docs.title: Auth0
docs.text:
Collects authentication and authorization event logs from Auth0 (Okta Customer Identity Cloud), including login events, failed authentication attempts, and admin audit logs.

Category Identity & Access Connector Name signal-client.auth0 Auth Method OAuth2 Client Credentials Polling Interval 5 min (logs); built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs Auth0 Management API

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

Active Auth0 subscription. Admin access required to create Machine-to-Machine applications.

  • Active Auth0 tenant
  • Admin access to the Auth0 Dashboard
  • Network: Conductor can reach your Auth0 domain on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Log in to the Auth0 Dashboard at https://manage.auth0.com/
  2. Navigate to Applications → Applications
  3. Click Create Application
  4. Select Machine to Machine Applications
  5. Name it (e.g., "WitFoo Conductor")
  6. Select the Auth0 Management API as the authorized API
  7. Grant the scope: read:logs
  8. Click Authorize
  9. Note the Domain, Client ID, and Client Secret from the application settings

Auth0 Domain Format

Your Auth0 domain has the format <your-tenant>.us.auth0.com (or .eu.auth0.com for EU tenants). Custom domains are also supported.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select Auth0
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Domain <tenant>.us.auth0.com Auth0 tenant domain Client ID <your-client-id> Machine-to-Machine app Client ID Client Secret <your-client-secret> Machine-to-Machine app secret

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep "auth0"

    Look for successful poll messages:

    [INFO] auth0: fetched <N> log events

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts from this source

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401)
docs.text:
• Verify the Client ID and Client Secret are correct
  • Ensure the application is authorized for the Management API with read:logs
  • Check that the Domain format is correct (include .auth0.com)

docs.title: Forbidden (403)
docs.text:
• The application may lack the read:logs scope
  • Re-authorize the application in Applications → select app → APIs tab → Auth0 Management API → add read:logs

docs.title: Rate Limited (429)
docs.text:
• Auth0 rate limits vary by plan tier (50 req/sec on free plan)
  • The polling interval is built in and cannot be changed
  • Conductor automatically implements exponential backoff

docs.title: Log Retention
docs.text:
• Auth0 log retention varies by plan:
    • Free: 2 days
    • Developer: 2 days
    • Developer Pro: 10 days
    • Enterprise: 30 days
  • If gaps appear in data, increase polling frequency to stay within retention window

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify authentication events exist: test by logging into your Auth0-powered app
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -I https://<tenant>.us.auth0.com

See also: Integration Catalog · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: AWS GuardDuty
docs.text:
Collects threat detection findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon's managed threat detection service that monitors for malicious activity and anomalous behavior across AWS accounts and workloads.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.aws-guardduty Auth Method IAM Access Key + Secret Key Polling Interval 10 min; built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs AWS GuardDuty API

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

Active AWS account with GuardDuty enabled. IAM permissions to create users and/or roles.

  • Active AWS account
  • GuardDuty enabled in the target region
  • IAM access to create users or roles
  • Network: Conductor can reach guardduty.<region>.amazonaws.com on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the AWS Console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/
  2. Navigate to IAM → Users → Create user
  3. Name the user (e.g., witfoo-guardduty-reader)
  4. Select Programmatic access (Access key)
  5. Attach the managed policy: AmazonGuardDutyReadOnlyAccess
  6. Complete user creation
  7. Copy the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key

Cross-Account Collection

For multi-account environments, create an IAM role with an external ID instead of an IAM user. The role should trust the Conductor account and have AmazonGuardDutyReadOnlyAccess attached.

docs.title: Enable GuardDuty (if not already enabled)
docs.text:
1. Navigate to GuardDuty in the AWS Console
  2. Click Get Started → Enable GuardDuty
  3. GuardDuty begins analyzing VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail events, and DNS logs

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select AWS GuardDuty
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Region us-east-1 AWS region where GuardDuty is enabled Access Key ID <your-access-key> IAM access key from step 1 Secret Access Key <your-secret-key> IAM secret key from step 1 Detector ID (optional) Leave blank for auto-discovery

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

Detector ID Auto-Discovery

If the Detector ID field is left blank, Conductor will automatically discover the GuardDuty detector in the configured region using the ListDetectors API.

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep "guardduty"

    Look for successful poll messages:

    [INFO] aws-guardduty: fetched <N> findings

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts from this source

GuardDuty Severity Scale

GuardDuty findings use a severity scale of 0–8.9. Conductor normalizes these to WitFoo severity levels automatically.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401/403)
docs.text:
• Verify the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key are correct
  • Ensure the IAM user has the AmazonGuardDutyReadOnlyAccess policy attached
  • Check that the IAM user or access key is not disabled

docs.title: Wrong Region
docs.text:
• GuardDuty is region-specific — ensure the Region field matches where GuardDuty is enabled
  • If GuardDuty is enabled in multiple regions, create one integration per region

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm GuardDuty is enabled in the target AWS region
  • GuardDuty may take up to 24 hours to generate initial findings
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -I https://guardduty.<region>.amazonaws.com

See also: Integration Catalog · AWS Security Hub · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: AWS Security Hub
docs.text:
Collects aggregated security findings from AWS Security Hub, which consolidates alerts from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer, Firewall Manager, and third-party tools into the AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF).

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.aws-securityhub Auth Method IAM Access Key + Secret Key Polling Interval 10 min; built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs AWS Security Hub API

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

Active AWS account with Security Hub enabled. IAM permissions to create users and/or roles.

  • Active AWS account
  • Security Hub enabled in the target region
  • IAM access to create users or roles
  • Network: Conductor can reach securityhub.<region>.amazonaws.com on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
If you already have AWS credentials for GuardDuty, you can reuse the same IAM user — just add the Security Hub policy.

  1. Sign in to the AWS Console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/
  2. Navigate to IAM → Users → Create user (or select existing user)
  3. Name the user (e.g., witfoo-securityhub-reader)
  4. Attach the managed policy: AWSSecurityHubReadOnlyAccess
  5. If using an existing GuardDuty IAM user, add this policy to the same user
  6. Create an Access Key (programmatic access)
  7. Copy the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key

docs.title: Enable Security Hub (if not already enabled)
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Security Hub in the AWS Console
  2. Click Go to Security Hub → Enable Security Hub
  3. Select security standards to enable (CIS, PCI DSS, AWS Foundational)

Security Hub vs GuardDuty

Security Hub aggregates findings from multiple AWS security services including GuardDuty. If you only need GuardDuty findings, use the AWS GuardDuty integration instead. Use both if you want findings from all integrated AWS security services.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select AWS Security Hub
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Region us-east-1 AWS region where Security Hub is enabled Access Key ID <your-access-key> IAM access key from step 1 Secret Access Key <your-secret-key> IAM secret key from step 1

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep "securityhub"

    Look for successful poll messages:

    [INFO] aws-securityhub: fetched <N> findings

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts from this source

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401/403)
docs.text:
• Verify the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key are correct
  • Ensure the IAM user has the AWSSecurityHubReadOnlyAccess policy attached
  • Check that the access key is active

docs.title: Wrong Region
docs.text:
• Security Hub is region-specific — configure one integration per region
  • Findings are not cross-region unless using Organizations delegated admin

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm Security Hub is enabled in the target region
  • Enable at least one security standard (CIS, PCI DSS) to generate findings
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -I https://securityhub.<region>.amazonaws.com

See also: Integration Catalog · AWS GuardDuty · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: AWS VPC Flow Logs
docs.text:
Pulls Amazon VPC flow log objects from S3, using SQS event notifications as the work queue, and summarizes them into network conversations with the same flow engine as the on-premises NetFlow/IPFIX collector.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.aws-vpc-flow-pull Auth Method IAM Access Key Polling Interval Drains the queue, then waits 5 min Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs Publish flow logs to Amazon S3

This connector pulls flow logs from AWS directly. It is separate from the awsvpcflow parser, which reads VPC flow lines that something else forwards over syslog.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

An AWS account with VPC flow logs, and IAM access to create a policy, a user or role with an access key, an S3 event notification and an SQS queue.

  • VPC flow logs published to an S3 bucket in text format (the default, gzip-compressed). Parquet delivery is not read
  • An S3 bucket whose name has no dots
  • An SQS queue that receives the bucket's ObjectCreated event notifications
  • Network: Conductor can reach the SQS and S3 endpoints of the region on port 443

docs.title: Publish Flow Logs and Notifications
docs.text:
1. Publish your VPC flow logs to an S3 bucket. Any flow log format is read, but prefer a custom format that includes flow-direction (a version 5 field). The default format has no direction column, so each record's client and server are decided from port numbers alone. For example:

    ${version} ${account-id} ${interface-id} ${srcaddr} ${dstaddr} ${srcport} ${dstport} ${protocol} ${packets} ${bytes} ${start} ${end} ${action} ${log-status} ${tcp-flags} ${pkt-srcaddr} ${pkt-dstaddr} ${flow-direction}

  2. Add an S3 event notification for ObjectCreated events that targets an SQS queue. Raw S3 notifications and SNS-wrapped delivery both work.

  3. Set the queue's default visibility timeout to at least 300 seconds. With a lower value (30 seconds is the AWS default), SQS delivers messages again while large objects are still being processed. Duplicates are detected and skipped, but the work is wasted.

docs.title: Grant Least-Privilege Access
docs.text:
Create an IAM user or role for the connector with only this policy, then create an access key for it. Replace the placeholders with your own values:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "sqs:ReceiveMessage",
        "sqs:DeleteMessage",
        "sqs:GetQueueAttributes"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:YOUR_QUEUE"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR_FLOW_LOG_BUCKET/*"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select AWS VPC Flow Logs
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Region us-east-1 AWS region of the queue and bucket Access Key ID (access key ID) IAM access key Secret Access Key (secret) IAM secret, never logged SQS Queue URL https://sqs.<region>.amazonaws.com/<account-id>/<queue-name> The queue that receives the S3 event notifications Log Format (optional) (blank) Used only for objects delivered without a header line. Each object's own header line always wins

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep -i "vpc"

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for network flow artifacts from this source

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: Each poll drains the queue: it keeps receiving until the queue is empty, up to 500 messages per cycle, then waits five minutes. A backlog that outlasts that is logged as vpc flow queue backlog. If you see it, split the flow logs across a second connector instance with its own queue.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401 or 403)
docs.text:
• Verify the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key
  • Check that the policy grants the three SQS actions on the queue and s3:GetObject on the bucket
  • Check that the Region matches the queue

docs.title: Bucket Name Contains a Dot
docs.text: • The connector reads objects at <bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com, and S3's certificate does not cover a dotted bucket name there, so the connection fails. The log says s3 bucket name contains a dot and the message stays on the queue. Deliver the flow logs to a bucket whose name has no dots

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Confirm the S3 event notification targets the queue named in the form
  • Confirm the flow log file format is text. Parquet objects are skipped, and the connector logs a warning with the count skipped
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

docs.title: Duplicate Deliveries
docs.text:
• Raise the queue's visibility timeout to at least 300 seconds

docs.title: Azure Security
docs.text:
Collects security and identity telemetry from Microsoft Azure via the Microsoft Graph API — Defender XDR incidents and alerts, Entra ID sign-in and directory audit logs, Identity Protection risk detections and risky users, and Microsoft Secure Score — providing visibility into cloud workload protection and identity threats.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.azure-security Auth Method OAuth2 (Azure AD — Client ID + Client Secret + Tenant ID) Polling Interval 1 min; built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs Microsoft Graph Security API

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

Active Microsoft Azure subscription with Microsoft Defender for Cloud or Microsoft 365 Defender. Azure AD admin access required to register an application.

  • Active Azure subscription with security services enabled
  • Global Administrator or Application Administrator role in Azure AD
  • Network: Conductor can reach graph.microsoft.com and login.microsoftonline.com on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Log in to the Azure Portal at https://portal.azure.com/
  2. Navigate to Azure Active Directory → App registrations → New registration
  3. Configure the application:
    • Name: WitFoo Conductor
    • Supported account types: Accounts in this organizational directory only
  4. Click Register
  5. Note the Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID from the overview page
  6. Navigate to Certificates & secrets → New client secret
    • Description: WitFoo Conductor
    • Expires: 24 months (recommended)
  7. Copy the Value (client secret) — it is only shown once

  8. Navigate to API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph → Application permissions, and add the following ten application permissions (all read-only):

    Permission Unlocks SecurityIncident.Read.All Defender incidents SecurityAlert.Read.All Defender alerts (v2) AuditLog.Read.All Entra ID sign-in and directory audit logs IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All Identity Protection risk detections IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All Identity Protection risky users SecurityEvents.Read.All Microsoft Secure Score SignInIdentifier.Read.All User Identifiers DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All Intune managed-device & detected-app inventory (CSC8 2/4) User.Read.All Entra ID user-account inventory (CSC8 5) Device.Read.All Entra ID registered/joined device inventory

    Inventory licensing

    User sign-in activity (signInActivity on /users) additionally requires Entra ID P1/P2 plus AuditLog.Read.All. The optional DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All unlocks Intune compliance/configuration policy detail for control 4. These inventory pulls are snapshots on an hourly cadence and auto-disable if the tenant lacks the license/permission — the rest keep flowing.

  9. Click Grant admin consent for your tenant and confirm every row shows Granted. Application permissions require admin consent, and any later change requires re-consent.

Store Credentials Securely

The client secret grants access to your Azure security data. Store it securely and do not share it in tickets or email.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select Azure Security
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance (e.g., "Azure Production Tenant")

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Tenant ID <your-tenant-id> Azure AD directory (tenant) ID Client ID <your-client-id> Application (client) ID from app registration Client Secret <your-client-secret> Secret value from step 1

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep "azure"

    Look for successful poll messages:

    [INFO] azure-security: fetched <N> events

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to the WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search page and search for artifacts from this source

First Poll Timing

The connector polls on a built-in schedule that cannot be changed (see Polling Interval above). Expect the first data within one interval of saving.

docs.title: Data Collection Details
docs.text:
Each polling cycle, the connector pulls twelve Microsoft Graph v1.0 endpoints. Every endpoint is collected independently: if your tenant is not licensed or permissioned for one, only that endpoint is skipped (and reported as unavailable) — the rest keep flowing. The four inventory endpoints are snapshots (the full list is re-pulled on an hourly cadence, not every cycle).

Check Graph endpoint Data Required permission License Incidents /security/incidents Correlated Defender XDR incidents SecurityIncident.Read.All Microsoft Defender XDR Alerts (v2) /security/alerts_v2 Defender alerts with typed evidence SecurityAlert.Read.All A Microsoft Defender product Sign-in logs /auditLogs/signIns Entra ID interactive sign-ins AuditLog.Read.All Entra ID P1 or P2 Directory audits /auditLogs/directoryAudits Entra ID directory change audit AuditLog.Read.All Entra ID (any; P1/P2 for 30-day retention) Risk detections /identityProtection/riskDetections Identity Protection risk events IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All Entra ID P2 Risky users /identityProtection/riskyUsers Identity Protection risky users IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All Entra ID P2 Secure Score /security/secureScores Microsoft Secure Score posture SecurityEvents.Read.All Microsoft 365 / Defender User Identifiers /users Identifier-related fields SignInIdentifier.Read.All Entra ID (any) / Microsoft 365 E5 Managed devices (snapshot) /deviceManagement/managedDevices Intune device inventory + compliance state DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All Microsoft Intune Detected apps (snapshot) /deviceManagement/detectedApps Intune installed-software inventory DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All Microsoft Intune Entra users (snapshot) /users User-account inventory (enabled, last sign-in) User.Read.All (+ AuditLog.Read.All) Entra ID (P1/P2 for sign-in activity) Entra devices (snapshot) /devices Registered/joined device inventory Device.Read.All Entra ID

docs.title: V2 Alert Evidence Types
docs.text:
The v2 alerts endpoint (/security/alerts_v2) returns structured evidence objects. The connector processes these typed evidence payloads:

Evidence Type Description Mailbox Compromised or targeted mailbox details Message Email message artifacts (subject, sender, recipients) URL Suspicious or malicious URL indicators MailCluster Grouped email cluster analysis data

Pagination is handled automatically via @odata.nextLink response links.

Rate Limiting Behavior

Microsoft Graph API returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. The connector implements a 10-minute cooldown with context-aware retry on 429 responses. HTTP 403 responses are handled silently (permission warning logged) to prevent blocking other data collection.

docs.title: Required API Permissions
docs.text:
Grant these ten Microsoft Graph application permissions (admin-consented) for full coverage of all twelve checks. *.Read.All is read-only and least-privilege, so the *.ReadWrite.All variants are never required.

Permission Type Unlocks SecurityIncident.Read.All Application Incidents SecurityAlert.Read.All Application Alerts (v2) AuditLog.Read.All Application Sign-in logs and directory audits IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All Application Risk detections IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All Application Risky users SecurityEvents.Read.All Application Secure Score SignInIdentifier.Read.All Application User Identifiers DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All Application Managed devices and detected apps (Intune inventory) User.Read.All Application Entra ID user-account inventory Device.Read.All Application Entra ID registered/joined device inventory

All ten require admin consent, and Microsoft does not apply a permission change until an administrator re-consents.

License-gated checks are expected, not errors

Some checks require a specific Microsoft license. Without Entra ID P2, Risk detections and Risky users are unavailable; without P1, Sign-in logs; without a Defender product, Incidents and Alerts. The connector keeps every licensed and permissioned check flowing and reports the rest as unavailable with the reason — add the matching license and confirm the permission is consented to enable a gated check.

docs.title: CSC8 Compliance Coverage
docs.text:
Once the Azure connector is collecting and the data reaches Analytics, these CIS Controls v8 (csc8) controls populate on the Compliance Reporting page, each attributed to the detecting Microsoft product:

CSC8 Control Detecting product Microsoft data source 1 — Inventory & Control of Enterprise Assets Microsoft Defender Defender for Endpoint device coverage (Intune/Entra device inventory supplements) 2 — Inventory & Control of Software Assets Microsoft Intune Detected apps 4 — Secure Configuration Microsoft Intune Managed-device compliance state 5 — Account Management Microsoft Entra ID User accounts 6 — Access Control Management Microsoft Entra ID Sign-in / directory audit 7 — Continuous Vulnerability Management Microsoft Defender Defender for Endpoint alerts 9 — Email & Web Browser Protections Microsoft Defender Defender for Office 365 alerts 10 — Malware Defenses Microsoft Defender Defender Antivirus / Endpoint alerts

Coverage appears once the product is detected

A control lights up only when its Microsoft product is detected in your environment (data flowing). Controls 1/5/6/7/9/10 activate from the Defender and Entra streams already collected above; controls 2 and 4 require the Intune device/app inventory permission (DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All) so the inventory snapshots flow. If a control still shows "No detection configured", confirm the integration is connected and the relevant permission is admin-consented — see Common Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401)
docs.text:
• Verify the Tenant ID, Client ID, and Client Secret are correct
  • Ensure the client secret has not expired
  • Check that the app registration exists in the correct Azure AD tenant
  • AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret provided — the configured secret is the Secret ID (a GUID), not the secret Value. Create a new client secret and paste the Value column; it is only visible at creation time. On Conductor releases before 1.8.2 this mistake produced no visible error (the connector silently retried every 5 seconds) — upgrade and the failure surfaces in integration health with this exact hint.

docs.title: Forbidden (403) on one or more checks
docs.text:
• A 403 affects only the specific check whose permission or license is missing — the other checks keep collecting.
  • Confirm the matching application permission from the table above is added and that admin consent has been (re-)granted — a permission added without re-consent still returns 403.
  • If the permission is consented, confirm the tenant holds the required license for that check (Entra ID P1/P2, or a Defender product).

docs.title: Rate Limited (429)
docs.text:
• Microsoft Graph API has per-app and per-tenant throttling limits
  • The polling interval is built in and cannot be changed
  • Conductor automatically implements exponential backoff on 429 responses

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Check Signal Client logs for errors: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -I https://graph.microsoft.com
  • Confirm security alerts exist in the Azure Security Center for the polling time window
  • Ensure Microsoft Defender for Cloud or another security service is generating alerts

See also: Integration Catalog · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: Azure VNet Flow Logs
docs.text:
Pulls Azure Network Watcher flow-log JSON blobs from a Storage account and summarizes them into network conversations with the same flow engine as the on-premises NetFlow/IPFIX collector. It can also read legacy NSG flow log records.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.azure-vnet-flow-pull Auth Method Microsoft Entra app (client credentials) or Storage SAS token Polling Interval 60 s Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs Virtual network flow logs

This connector is separate from Azure Security (Microsoft Graph alerts) and Microsoft Sentinel (incidents).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

An Azure subscription with Network Watcher flow logs written to a Storage account, and permission to grant read access to that account.

  • Virtual network flow logs (or legacy NSG flow logs) written to a Storage account
  • Permission to create a Microsoft Entra app registration and assign it a role, or to create a SAS token
  • Network: Conductor can reach the Storage account and, for an Entra app, Microsoft Entra ID, on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text: Choose one way to authenticate.

docs.title: Option A: Microsoft Entra App (Recommended)
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, register an application in Microsoft Entra ID
  2. Copy the Directory (tenant) ID and the Application (client) ID
  3. Under Certificates & secrets, create a client secret and copy its Value (not the secret ID). It is shown once
  4. On the Storage account, assign the app the Storage Blob Data Reader role. Grant nothing broader

docs.title: Option B: Storage SAS Token
docs.text:
1. On the Storage account, create a SAS token for the flow-log container
  2. Grant Read and List only
  3. Copy the SAS token

docs.title: Find the Container
docs.text:
Flow log Container Virtual network flow logs insights-logs-flowlogflowevent Legacy NSG flow logs insights-logs-networksecuritygroupflowevent

Configure one integration for each container.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select Azure VNet Flow Logs
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Storage Account (account name) The account that receives the flow logs: 3–24 lowercase letters and numbers Container insights-logs-flowlogflowevent The flow-log container Blob Prefix (optional) (blank) Only blobs whose name starts with this text are read. Leave empty to read the whole container Azure Cloud Public (core.windows.net) Or US Government (core.usgovcloudapi.net), or China 21Vianet (core.chinacloudapi.cn) Authentication Microsoft Entra app (client credentials) Or Storage SAS token Directory (tenant) ID (tenant ID) Entra app only Application (client) ID (client ID) Entra app only Client Secret (secret value) Entra app only. Enter the secret VALUE, not the secret ID SAS Token (SAS token) SAS only. A read and list SAS for the container Also accept legacy NSG Flow Log records On Read legacy NSG flow log records too. On by default for a new integration

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

Blob Prefix is case-sensitive

The prefix is compared exactly with the start of each blob name, upper and lower case included. Virtual network flow-log blob names start with flowLogResourceID=/, then the subscription ID in upper case, then _NETWORKWATCHERRG/NETWORKWATCHER_, the region and the flow log's name. The portal shows the subscription ID in lower case, which matches nothing. Legacy NSG names start with resourceId=/SUBSCRIPTIONS/. A prefix that matches nothing is not an error: the connector logs one warning and reads nothing.

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep -i "azure"

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for network flow artifacts from this source

docs.title: How Reading Works
docs.text:
• Each blob is read forward from a saved position. A record Azure has only partly written is left unread and picked up on a later cycle.
  • At most 32 blobs are read per cycle. This is a limit of the connector, not of Azure. In a very large container, a blob can wait several cycles for its turn.
  • Blobs not modified within the last 24 hours are not read, so a connector stopped for longer than that does not fill the gap.
  • Records refused while legacy NSG acceptance was off are not read again when you turn it on.

NSG flow logs retire

Microsoft retires NSG flow logs on 30 September 2027. Move to virtual network flow logs.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401 or 403)
docs.text:
• Entra app: verify the tenant ID, client ID and secret value, and that the app has Storage Blob Data Reader on the Storage account
  • SAS: verify the token grants Read and List on the container and has not expired
  • Check that Azure Cloud matches the cloud of the Storage account

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Confirm the Container is the one your flow logs write to
  • Check the Blob Prefix: the subscription ID must be in upper case. Clear the prefix to read the whole container
  • For legacy NSG records, turn on Also accept legacy NSG Flow Log records
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

See also: Integration Catalog · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: Carbon Black
docs.text:
Collects endpoint alerts and device inventory from VMware Carbon Black Cloud (now Broadcom), including malware detections, suspicious activity alerts, and endpoint asset data.

Category Endpoint Security Connector Name signal-client.carbon-black Auth Method API Key + API ID (X-Auth-Token) Polling Interval 10 min (alerts), 1 hr (devices); built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs Carbon Black Cloud API

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Log in to the Carbon Black Cloud Console at https://defense.conferdeploy.net/ (or your regional instance)
  2. Navigate to Settings → API Access
  3. Click Add API Key
  4. Select Custom as the access level type
  5. Set permissions: org.alerts: READ
  6. Name the key (e.g., "WitFoo Conductor")
  7. Click Save
  8. Copy the API ID and API Secret Key
  9. Note the Org Key from Settings → API Access (shown at the top)

API Key Types

Carbon Black Cloud has multiple API key types: API, SIEM, and Custom. Use Custom type with specific read permissions for WitFoo integration. SIEM keys provide different endpoint access.

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

Finding Your Org Key

The Org Key is displayed at the top of the Settings → API Access page in the Carbon Black Cloud console. It is a short alphanumeric string (e.g., ABCD1234).

docs.title: Cloudflare
docs.text:
Collects Cloudflare account audit logs and per-zone WAF and firewall events with a scoped API token.

Category Network Security Connector Name signal-client.cloudflare-security-events Auth Method API Token (scoped) Polling Interval 5 min Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs Create API token

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

A Cloudflare account, and permission to create API tokens. The scoped token works on every Cloudflare plan for audit and firewall events.

  • Cloudflare account with the zones you want to collect from
  • Permission to create a custom API token
  • Your 32-character Account ID and the Zone IDs of the zones to collect
  • Network: Conductor can reach api.cloudflare.com on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
Create a custom API token that grants only what each data family needs.

  1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, open My Profile → API Tokens
  2. Click Create Token, then choose a Custom token

  3. Add the permissions for the families you will collect:

    Family Permission Audit logs Account → Account Settings → Read Firewall events Account → Account Analytics → Read, with the zones you want under Zone Resources

  4. Create the token and copy it. It is shown once.

  5. Copy the Account ID and each Zone ID from the dashboard

Use a scoped token

The legacy Global API Key is not supported, because it cannot be scoped down. If you collect audit logs only, the Account Analytics permission is not needed.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select Cloudflare
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description API Token (paste token) The scoped API token from step 1 Account ID 32 hex characters Account ID from the Cloudflare dashboard Zone IDs <zone-id-1>,<zone-id-2> Comma-separated 32-character Zone IDs, at most 40. Required when Collect Firewall Events is on Collect Audit Logs On Poll account audit logs (Audit Logs v2). On by default Collect Firewall Events On Poll WAF and firewall events for each zone. On by default

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

More than 40 zones

Each zone costs at least one query per cycle, so one instance takes at most 40 zones. Split a larger estate across more instances (up to 5).

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep -i "cloudflare"

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts from this source

docs.title: Data Sources
docs.text:
Source Data Type Default Interval Audit Logs v2 Account audit events 5 min Firewall events (firewallEventsAdaptive) WAF and firewall events, per zone 5 min

Zero Trust Gateway events are not collected

Every Gateway dataset Cloudflare documents for its GraphQL Analytics API is an aggregate, so the connector does not collect Zero Trust Gateway events.

Lookback after an outage

A zone with no saved position starts at the last hour. After an outage longer than 24 hours, the connector asks for the last 24 hours only, so the older part of the gap is not collected. The skipped span is logged as a warning that names both ends.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401 or 403)
docs.text:
Cloudflare answers a wrong Account ID, a zone the token cannot read, a token without the permission a family needs, and a revoked token with the same two statuses. The instance shows Failure with the health code auth_failed, and is retried after 15 minutes.

  • Check that the Account ID and Zone IDs belong to the token's account
  • Check that the token carries the permission for each enabled family
  • Check that the token is a scoped API token, not a Global API Key

docs.title: Rate Limited (429)
docs.text:
• A 429 ends the polling cycle, and the connector waits for the time Cloudflare gives in Retry-After before the next poll
  • Other dashboards, tokens or tools that use the same Cloudflare user share its API budget. Reduce their use, or split zones across instances

docs.title: One Bad Zone Stops the Instance
docs.text: • A Zone ID that is not found, or that the token cannot read, fails the whole instance for 15 minutes at a time, including the audit logs and the other zones. Correct or remove the zone

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Confirm Collect Firewall Events has at least one Zone ID
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

docs.title: Common Integration Troubleshooting
docs.text: This guide covers issues common to all Signal Client pull-based integrations. For vendor-specific troubleshooting, see the individual integration guides.

docs.title: Cannot Reach Vendor API
docs.text:
Conductor must have outbound HTTPS (port 443) access to the vendor's API endpoints. Verify connectivity from the Conductor host:

# Test basic connectivity
curl -I https://<vendor-api-endpoint>

# If behind a forward proxy
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy:port
curl -I https://<vendor-api-endpoint>

If your environment uses a forward proxy, configure it in the Conductor node settings via wfa configure.

docs.title: TLS Certificate Errors
docs.text:
If the vendor API endpoint uses a certificate signed by a private CA:

  1. Copy the CA certificate to /witfoo/certs/
  2. Run sudo wfa configure and update the CA certificate path

  3. Restart Signal Client:

    docker restart signal-client-svc

docs.title: DNS Resolution Failures
docs.text:
If Signal Client logs show DNS errors:

  1. Verify the Conductor host can resolve the vendor hostname:

    nslookup <vendor-api-endpoint>

  2. Check /etc/resolv.conf for correct upstream DNS servers

  3. If using internal DNS, ensure the vendor domain is not blocked

docs.title: Token Expired
docs.text:
Most API tokens have expiration dates. If a previously working integration stops collecting data:

  1. Check Signal Client logs for 401 errors:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100 | grep "401"

  2. Generate a new token in the vendor console

  3. Update the credentials in the Conductor UI → Integrations
  4. Click Save — new credentials take effect within seconds via NATS KV watch

docs.title: OAuth2 Token Refresh Failures
docs.text:
For OAuth2 integrations (Microsoft, CrowdStrike, Sophos, Wiz, etc.):

  • Verify the Client ID and Client Secret are correct
  • Check that the application/service principal has not been deleted
  • Confirm required API scopes/permissions are still granted
  • Some vendors require admin consent to be re-granted after scope changes

docs.title: IP Allowlist
docs.text:
Some vendors restrict API access by source IP address:

  1. Determine the Conductor host's public IP
  2. Add it to the vendor's API allowlist (often in Settings → API → IP Restrictions)
  3. If Conductor uses a NAT gateway, add the NAT IP instead

docs.title: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
docs.text:
Signal Client implements automatic exponential backoff on 429 responses. If you see persistent rate limiting:

  1. Let the backoff work — polling intervals are built into each connector and cannot be changed (Splunk's excepted). After a 429, Signal Client waits as long as the vendor's Retry-After header asks (up to 15 minutes), or up to 10 minutes when there is none
  2. Reduce concurrent integrations — if many integrations poll the same vendor simultaneously

  3. Check vendor rate limits — each vendor has different quotas:

    Vendor Typical Rate Limit CrowdStrike 100 req/min Microsoft Graph 10,000 req/10min Okta 600 req/min Tenable 300-500 req/min SentinelOne 1000 req/min Qualys 300 req/hr

  4. Contact the vendor to request a rate limit increase if needed

docs.title: No Artifacts Appearing
docs.text:
1. Verify the integration is Enabled in the Conductor UI

  2. Check for errors in Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

  3. Verify data exists in the vendor console for the polling time window

  4. Check the NATS JetStream stream:

    docker exec broker-edge-svc nats stream info DATA

  5. Confirm Artifact Exporter is running and connected to Analytics:

    docker logs artifact-exporter-svc --tail=50

docs.title: Duplicate Artifacts
docs.text:
WitFoo's ProtoGraph deduplication in the Artifact Filter service automatically reduces duplicate events. If you see excessive duplicates:

  1. Check if multiple integration instances are configured for the same vendor account
  2. Verify checkpoint tracking is working (Signal Client resumes from the last successful position)

docs.title: Missing Events
docs.text:
If some events appear but others are missing:

  1. Check the vendor's data retention settings — some APIs only return recent data
  2. Verify the API credentials have permissions for all required data types
  3. Some integrations collect multiple data types on different schedules (for example alerts every 10 minutes and assets every hour; each guide lists its connector's schedule)

docs.title: High Memory Usage
docs.text:
If Signal Client shows elevated memory usage:

  • Reduce the number of concurrent polling integrations
  • Check for vendors that return large batch responses (thousands of records per page)

docs.title: Slow Polling
docs.text:
Common causes of slow poll cycles:

  • Network latency to the vendor API endpoint
  • Large data volumes — consider narrower time windows or more frequent polling to keep batch sizes small
  • Vendor API rate limiting — 429 responses trigger backoff delays
  • DNS resolution delays — verify DNS is fast from the Conductor host

docs.title: Diagnostic Commands
docs.text:
Quick reference for troubleshooting from the Conductor host:

# Signal Client logs (last 100 lines)
docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

# Signal Client logs filtered by integration
docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=200 | grep "<connector-name>"

# Check container health
docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.Status}}' signal-client-svc

# NATS stream statistics
docker exec broker-edge-svc nats stream info DATA

# Test outbound connectivity to a vendor
curl -sI -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://<vendor-api-endpoint>

# Check container resource usage
docker stats signal-client-svc --no-stream

See also: Integration Catalog · Signal Client · General Conductor Troubleshooting

• Verify the Public Token and Private Token are correct
  • Ensure the API token has not been revoked in Darktrace
  • Clock skew between Conductor and Darktrace can cause HMAC signature failures — ensure both systems use NTP

docs.title: Network Connectivity
docs.text:

  • If using a self-signed TLS certificate on the appliance, see Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: Forbidden (403)
docs.text:

  • Create a new token with broader permissions

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Verify model breaches exist in the Darktrace Threat Visualizer
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

docs.text:
Collects threat event data from Deep Instinct's deep learning-based endpoint protection platform, providing visibility into malware prevention, detection events, and device inventory.

First Poll Timing

docs.title: DNS Zone Transfer
docs.text:
Collects DNS zone records via AXFR (Authoritative Zone Transfer), providing visibility into DNS infrastructure, record changes, and domain inventory.

Category Infrastructure Connector Name signal-client.dns-zone-transfer Auth Method None (AXFR protocol) Polling Interval 1 min; built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs RFC 5936 — DNS Zone Transfer Protocol

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirements

Your DNS server must allow AXFR zone transfers from the Conductor host's IP address. This is a server configuration, not a vendor subscription.

  • DNS server(s) configured to allow AXFR transfers
  • Conductor host IP address allowlisted for zone transfers
  • Network: Conductor can reach DNS server(s) on port 53 (TCP)

docs.title: Step 1: Configure DNS Server for AXFR
docs.text:
Zone transfer configuration varies by DNS server software. Ensure the Conductor host is authorized.

BINDWindows DNSInfoblox

In named.conf, add the Conductor IP to allow-transfer: 

zone "example.com" {
    type master;
    file "/etc/bind/zones/example.com.zone";
    allow-transfer { <conductor-ip>; };
};

  1. Open DNS Manager
  2. Right-click the zone → Properties → Zone Transfers tab
  3. Select Allow zone transfers → Only to the following servers
  4. Add the Conductor host IP address
  1. Navigate to Data Management → DNS → Zones
  2. Edit the zone → Zone Transfers tab
  3. Add the Conductor host IP to the Allow Transfer list

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select DNS Zone Transfer
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description DNS Server IP 10.0.1.53 Primary DNS server address Forward Lookup Zones example.com,internal.local Comma-separated zone names

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator after the first transfer

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep "dns-zone-transfer"

    Look for successful transfer messages:

    [INFO] dns-zone-transfer: fetched <N> records

  3. Test manually — Verify AXFR works from the Conductor host:

    dig @10.0.1.53 example.com AXFR

First Poll Timing

The connector runs its zone transfers on a built-in schedule that cannot be changed (see Polling Interval above). Expect the first data within one interval of saving.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401)
docs.text:
• DNS zone transfers do not use authentication — this error is not applicable
  • If access is denied, see Forbidden below

docs.title: Forbidden (403)
docs.text:
• The DNS server is refusing the zone transfer
  • Verify the Conductor host IP is in the server's allow-transfer list
  • Check DNS server logs for transfer denied messages

docs.title: Rate Limited (429)
docs.text:
• DNS zone transfers are not rate limited in the traditional sense
  • However, very frequent transfers may impact DNS server performance
  • The connector runs a full zone transfer (AXFR) of each configured domain about once a minute (built in, not configurable); if that load matters for your DNS server, contact WitFoo support

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Check Signal Client logs for errors: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify network connectivity on TCP port 53 to the DNS server
  • Test manually: dig @<dns-server> <zone> AXFR
  • Ensure the zone names are spelled correctly

See also: Integration Catalog · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: Fortinet FortiAnalyzer
docs.text:
Collects log and event data from Fortinet FortiAnalyzer, the centralized logging and analytics platform for Fortinet security fabric devices.

Category Network Security Connector Name signal-client.fortianalyzer Auth Method Session Token (JSON-RPC) Polling Interval 10 min (traffic logs), 1 hr (event logs); built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs FortiAnalyzer REST API

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

Active FortiAnalyzer deployment (physical or virtual appliance). Admin access to create API administrator accounts.

  • Active FortiAnalyzer instance (v7.0+)
  • Admin access to the FortiAnalyzer web UI
  • ADOM (Administrative Domain) name
  • Network: Conductor can reach the FortiAnalyzer IP on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Log in to the FortiAnalyzer web UI at https://<fortianalyzer-ip>/
  2. Navigate to System Settings → Admin → Administrators
  3. Click Create New
  4. Set the Admin Profile to Standard_User or a custom read-only profile
  5. Configure the following:
    • Username and password
    • Enable JSON API Access (set to Read-Only)
    • Restrict Trusted Hosts to the Conductor IP if desired
  6. Click OK to save

ADOM Concept

FortiAnalyzer uses Administrative Domains (ADOMs) to organize logs by customer or network segment. Use root for the default domain, or specify the ADOM that contains the logs you want to collect.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select FortiAnalyzer
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Host <fortianalyzer-ip> FortiAnalyzer IP or hostname Username <your-username> API admin from step 1 Password <your-password> API admin password ADOM root Administrative Domain (default: root)

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    Look for successful session messages:

    [INFO] fortianalyzer: session established, fetching logs

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts from this source

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401)
docs.text:
• Verify the Username and Password are correct
  • Ensure JSON API Access is enabled for the admin account
  • Check that the admin account is not locked

docs.title: Forbidden (403)
docs.text:
• The admin profile may not have read access to the specified ADOM
  • Verify the admin has access to the target ADOM in FortiAnalyzer

docs.title: Session Timeout
docs.text:
• FortiAnalyzer sessions have configurable idle timeouts
  • Conductor handles automatic re-authentication when sessions expire
  • If persistent failures occur, check admin session settings in FortiAnalyzer

docs.title: Wrong ADOM
docs.text:
• If data appears from the wrong devices, verify the ADOM field
  • Use root for the default domain
  • List available ADOMs in FortiAnalyzer under System Settings → All ADOMs

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:

  • Check the FortiAnalyzer has devices forwarding logs to it
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -k https://<fortianalyzer-ip>/jsonrpc

docs.title: Google Cloud Security Command Center
docs.text:
Collects security findings from Google Cloud Security Command Center (SCC), Google's centralized security and risk management platform for GCP resources.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.gcp-scc Auth Method Service Account JSON Key Polling Interval 10 min (findings), 1 hr (source list); built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes Vendor Docs SCC API Documentation

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

Active Google Cloud organization with Security Command Center enabled (Standard or Premium tier). Organization-level access required.

  • Active Google Cloud organization (not just a project)
  • SCC Standard or Premium tier enabled
  • IAM access to create service accounts
  • Network: Conductor can reach securitycenter.googleapis.com on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the Google Cloud Console at https://console.cloud.google.com/
  2. Select the project where you want to create the service account
  3. Navigate to IAM & Admin → Service Accounts
  4. Click Create Service Account
  5. Name the account (e.g., witfoo-scc-reader)
  6. Click Create and Continue
  7. Grant the role Security Center Findings Viewer (roles/securitycenter.findingsViewer)
  8. Click Done
  9. Select the new service account → Keys tab → Add Key → Create New Key → JSON
  10. Download the JSON key file

Organization-Level Access

SCC operates at the organization level, not the project level. The service account must have the Findings Viewer role granted at the organization level in IAM.

docs.title: Grant Organization-Level Access
docs.text:
1. Navigate to IAM & Admin → IAM at the organization level
  2. Click Grant Access
  3. Enter the service account email
  4. Assign role: Security Center Findings Viewer
  5. Click Save

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select Google Cloud SCC
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Organization ID <your-org-id> GCP organization numeric ID API Key (paste full JSON key) Service account JSON key content

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

Finding Your Organization ID

Navigate to Cloud Identity → Account → Account Settings or run: gcloud organizations list

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep "gcp-scc"

    Look for successful poll messages:

    [INFO] gcp-scc: fetched <N> findings

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts from this source

docs.title: Verify Credentials Locally
docs.text:
# Test the service account key (optional, from any machine with gcloud)
gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=<key-file>.json
gcloud scc findings list <organization-id> --source="-" --limit=5

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401)
docs.text:
• Verify the JSON key content was pasted correctly (including all fields)
  • Ensure the service account has not been deleted or disabled
  • Regenerate the key if needed

docs.title: Forbidden (403)
docs.text:
• The service account likely lacks organization-level IAM binding
  • Grant Security Center Findings Viewer at the organization level, not the project level
  • Verify: gcloud organizations get-iam-policy <org-id>

docs.title: SCC Tier Limitations
docs.text:
• Standard tier provides limited finding types (Security Health Analytics)
  • Premium tier adds Event Threat Detection, Container Threat Detection, etc.
  • Check your SCC tier under Security → Security Command Center → Settings

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm SCC is enabled at the organization level
  • Enable security sources (Security Health Analytics, Event Threat Detection)
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -I https://securitycenter.googleapis.com

docs.title: GCP VPC Flow Logs
docs.text:
Pulls Google Cloud VPC flow log records from a Pub/Sub subscription, fed by a Cloud Logging sink, and summarizes them into network conversations with the same flow engine as the on-premises NetFlow/IPFIX collector and AWS VPC Flow Logs.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.gcp-vpc-flow-pull Auth Method Service Account JSON Polling Interval 2 min Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs About VPC Flow Logs records

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

A Google Cloud project with VPC Flow Logs, and IAM permission to create a Cloud Logging sink, a Pub/Sub topic and subscription, and a service account.

  • VPC Flow Logs enabled on the subnets you want visibility into
  • Permission to create a Cloud Logging sink, a Pub/Sub topic and a pull subscription
  • Permission to create a service account and a key for it
  • Network: Conductor can reach the Google Cloud APIs (*.googleapis.com) on port 443

docs.title: Route Flow Logs to Pub/Sub
docs.text:
1. Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnets you want to collect

  2. Create a Cloud Logging sink to a Pub/Sub topic with this filter:

    resource.type="gce_subnetwork" AND logName:"logs/compute.googleapis.com%2Fvpc_flows"

  3. Create a pull subscription on that topic

docs.title: Create a Service Account
docs.text:
1. Create a service account for the connector
  2. Grant it roles/pubsub.subscriber on the subscription only. The connector only pulls and acknowledges messages, so it needs nothing more
  3. Create a JSON key for the service account and download it

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select GCP VPC Flow Logs
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Project ID my-gcp-project The project that owns the Pub/Sub subscription Pub/Sub Subscription vpc-flows-sub The subscription ID, or the full projects/PROJECT/subscriptions/NAME path the console shows Service Account Key (JSON) (paste key file) The whole downloaded key file. It is stored with the integration's settings and never written to a log

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep -i "gcp"

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for network flow artifacts from this source

No TCP flags

The VPC Flow Logs record format carries byte and packet counts but no TCP flag field, so the SYN, RST and FIN counters are zero for this source. A zero there means "not reported by GCP", not "none observed".

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401 or 403)
docs.text:
• Paste the whole service account key file, including the braces
  • Check that the service account has roles/pubsub.subscriber on the subscription
  • Check that Project ID is the project that owns the subscription

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Confirm the Cloud Logging sink uses the filter above and writes to the topic the subscription is attached to
  • Confirm the subscription is a pull subscription
  • Check Signal Client logs: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100

docs.title: Pulls Pause for Ten Minutes
docs.text:
• One failed hand-off of the connector's output to the pipeline pauses its pulls for ten minutes. This is a known limit of this release; collection resumes on its own

See also: Integration Catalog · Integration Management · Signal Client · Common Troubleshooting

docs.title: HTTP/HTTPS Monitor
docs.text:
Probes the web endpoints you list and records response time, status code and TLS certificate expiry. A confirmed change from up to down raises a Service Disruption.

Category Infrastructure Connector Name signal-client.http-poll Auth Method None (no credentials are sent) Polling Interval Per target: 60 s by default, 30 s minimum Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

HTTP or HTTPS endpoints that answer without sign-in, such as a health or status URL.

  • An http or https URL for each endpoint to monitor
  • Network: Conductor can reach each endpoint on its port

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
The monitor sends no credentials, so there is nothing to create. Choose an endpoint that answers without sign-in, such as a health-check URL, and note the status codes that mean "up" for it.

No credentials in URLs

A URL that carries a user name or password (user:pass@) is refused.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select HTTP/HTTPS Monitor
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. For each endpoint, fill in a target. Click Add Target to add another:

    Field Value Description URL https://app.example.com/health Full http or https URL, with no credentials Label Billing API Optional friendly name. Defaults to the URL's host Method GET GET or HEAD Poll Interval (seconds) 60 Minimum 30. A lower value is raised to 30 Timeout (seconds) 10 Must be shorter than the interval Expected Status 200-399 Codes or ranges counted as up, for example 200-399 or 200,301,302

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

An instance holds up to 512 targets.

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep -i "http"

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for artifacts of stream http_monitor

docs.title: What It Records
docs.text:
Every check produces one artifact with the action http_up, http_down or cert_expiring. It carries the response time, the HTTP status, the label and, for HTTPS, the days until the certificate expires.

When a target fails 2 checks in a row after being up, the monitor emits one Service Disruption artifact. A single failed check never does. While the target stays down, it repeats at most once every 60 minutes. On a Docker Compose stack you can change these with HTTP_POLL_CONFIRM_CHECKS and HTTP_POLL_COOLDOWN_MINUTES on the signal client.

Redirects are recorded, not followed

A 30x answer is the recorded status. The monitor never follows the redirect, so list the final URL if that is what you want to watch.

docs.title: Target Always Down
docs.text:
• Check that the Conductor can reach the URL, and resolve its host name
  • Check Expected Status: a status outside it, such as a 401 with the default 200-399, counts as down
  • Raise Timeout (seconds) for a slow endpoint, keeping it below the interval

docs.title: URL Refused

docs.title: Microsoft Sentinel
docs.text:
Pulls security incidents from a Microsoft Sentinel workspace via the Azure Management (ARM) incidents API, bringing Sentinel's correlated incident data — including incidents raised by your Sentinel analytics rules — into the WitFoo pipeline.

Category Cloud Security / SIEM Connector Name signal-client.ms-sentinel Auth Method OAuth2 client credentials (Azure AD — Tenant ID + Client ID + Client Secret) Token Scope https://management.azure.com/.default Polling Interval 1 min; built in, not configurable Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs Microsoft Sentinel Incidents REST API

This is the PULL connector

This page covers pulling incidents from Sentinel into WitFoo. For pushing WitFoo detections and dashboards to Sentinel, see Microsoft Sentinel detection rules. For collecting Defender XDR / Entra ID telemetry via Microsoft Graph, see Azure Security — a separate connector with different permissions.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

A Microsoft Sentinel workspace (Log Analytics workspace with Sentinel enabled). Azure AD access sufficient to register an application and assign an Azure RBAC role on the workspace's resource group.

  • Microsoft Sentinel enabled on a Log Analytics workspace
  • Permission to register an Azure AD application and assign RBAC roles
  • Network: Conductor can reach management.azure.com and login.microsoftonline.com on port 443

docs.title: Step 1: Create API Credentials
docs.text:
1. Log in to the Azure Portal at https://portal.azure.com/
  2. Navigate to Microsoft Entra ID → App registrations → New registration
  3. Configure the application:
    • Name: WitFoo Conductor Sentinel
    • Supported account types: Accounts in this organizational directory only
  4. Click Register
  5. Note the Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID from the overview page
  6. Navigate to Certificates & secrets → New client secret
    • Description: WitFoo Conductor Sentinel
    • Expires: 24 months (recommended)
  7. Copy the secret Value — it is only shown once

Secret Value, not Secret ID

Copy the secret Value column, not the Secret ID (a GUID). Pasting the Secret ID is the most common setup mistake and fails with AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret provided.

docs.title: Step 2: Assign the Azure RBAC Role
docs.text:
No Graph API permissions needed

Unlike Azure Security, this connector needs no Microsoft Graph API permissions and no admin consent. Authorization is entirely through Azure RBAC: one role assignment on the resource group.

  1. Navigate to the resource group that contains your Sentinel workspace
  2. Open Access control (IAM) → Add → Add role assignment
  3. Role: Microsoft Sentinel Reader
  4. Assign access to: User, group, or service principal → select the WitFoo Conductor Sentinel app registration
  5. Click Review + assign

RBAC propagation can take up to 60 minutes

Azure role assignments can take up to an hour to propagate. A 403 AuthorizationFailed immediately after assignment is expected — wait and let the connector retry before changing anything.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select Microsoft Sentinel
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance (e.g., "Sentinel Production")

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Tenant ID <your-tenant-id> Azure AD directory (tenant) ID Client ID <your-client-id> Application (client) ID from Step 1 Client Secret <your-client-secret> Secret Value from Step 1 Subscription ID <your-subscription-id> Subscription containing the workspace Resource Group <your-resource-group> Resource group containing the workspace Workspace Name <your-workspace-name> Log Analytics workspace name (not the workspace GUID)

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

docs.title: Step 4: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 2>&1 | grep -i sentinel

    Look for: successfully authenticated with sentinel client

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to the WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search page and search for artifacts from this source

The connector checkpoints on incident lastModifiedTimeUtc, so each poll fetches only incidents created or modified since the previous poll.

docs.title: AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret provided
docs.text:
• The configured secret is the Secret ID (a GUID), not the secret Value. Create a new client secret and paste the Value column — the value is only visible at creation time.
  • On Conductor releases before 1.8.2 the sibling Azure Security connector showed no error at all for this mistake — upgrade and the failure becomes visible in integration health with this exact hint.

docs.title: Authentication Failed (401)
docs.text:
• Verify the Tenant ID, Client ID, and Client Secret are correct
  • Ensure the client secret has not expired
  • Check that the app registration exists in the correct Azure AD tenant

docs.title: AuthorizationFailed (403)
docs.text:
The token was issued but the service principal cannot read Sentinel incidents:

{"error":{"code":"AuthorizationFailed","message":"The client '<appId>' with object id '<oid>' does not have authorization to perform action 'Microsoft.SecurityInsights/incidents/read' over scope '/subscriptions/…/resourceGroups/…'"}}
  • Assign Microsoft Sentinel Reader on the workspace's resource group (Step 2) — a Graph permission or a role on a different scope does not grant this
  • If the role was just assigned, wait for RBAC propagation (up to 60 minutes)
  • Verify the Subscription ID, Resource Group, and Workspace Name point at the workspace that actually holds the role assignment

docs.title: Rate Limited (429)
docs.text:
• The Azure Management API throttles per-principal and per-subscription
  • The connector cools down for 10 minutes and resumes automatically
  • The polling interval is built in and cannot be changed

docs.title: No Data Appearing
docs.text:
• Confirm the integration shows Enabled in the Conductor UI
  • Check Signal Client logs for errors: docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=100
  • Verify network connectivity: curl -I https://management.azure.com
  • Confirm incidents exist in Sentinel → Threat management → Incidents for the polling window — the connector pulls incidents, not raw log rows

See also: Integration Catalog · Azure Security · Sentinel detection rules (push) · Integration Management · Common Troubleshooting

Broadest Collection

docs.title: OCI VCN Flow Logs
docs.text:
Pulls Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VCN flow log records from OCI Logging, through the Logging Search API with OCI request signing, and summarizes them into network conversations with the same flow engine as the on-premises NetFlow/IPFIX collector and AWS VPC Flow Logs.

Category Cloud Security Connector Name signal-client.oci-vcn-flow-pull Auth Method API Key (RSA Signing) Polling Interval 5 min Multi-Instance Yes (up to 5) Vendor Docs VCN flow logs

This connector collects flow logs. For audit events, logging data and Cloud Guard problems, see Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Vendor Requirements

An active OCI tenancy with VCN flow logs, and IAM permission to create users, groups, policies and API keys.

  • VCN flow logs enabled on the subnets or VNICs you want to collect
  • IAM access to create a user, a group, a policy and an API signing key
  • Network: Conductor can reach logging.<region>.oci.oraclecloud.com on port 443

docs.title: Generate an API Signing Key
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the OCI Console
  2. Create a dedicated user for the connector, and a group that contains it
  3. On the user, open API Keys and click Add API Key
  4. Select Generate API Key Pair, download the private key, and click Add
  5. Copy the fingerprint displayed

Unencrypted key

The private key must be unencrypted PEM. A passphrase-protected key is refused with an explicit message.

docs.title: Grant Least-Privilege Policies
docs.text:
Create a policy for the group, scoped to the compartment that holds the flow log group:

Allow group <your-group> to read log-content in compartment <your-compartment>
Allow group <your-group> to read log-groups in compartment <your-compartment>

docs.title: Collect Required OCIDs
docs.text: Value Where to Find Tenancy OCID Governance → Tenancy Details → OCID User OCID Identity → Users → select user → OCID Compartment OCID The compartment that holds the flow log group Log Group OCID The log group of the VCN flow log Flow Log OCID The VCN flow log itself

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Conductor
docs.text:
1. Open the Conductor UI at https://<conductor-ip>/admin/settings/integrations
  2. From the Add Integration dropdown, select OCI VCN Flow Logs
  3. Enter a unique name for this instance

  4. Fill in the settings form:

    Field Value Description Region us-ashburn-1 Lowercase OCI region identifier. A value with a dot, a slash or an @ is refused Tenancy OCID ocid1.tenancy.oc1..<id> From Tenancy Details User OCID ocid1.user.oc1..<id> The API user whose signing key you supply API Key Fingerprint aa:bb:cc:... Fingerprint from step 1 API Private Key (PEM) (paste PEM content) Unencrypted RSA signing key. Never written to a log Compartment OCID ocid1.compartment.oc1..<id> The compartment holding the flow log group Log Group OCID ocid1.loggroup.oc1.<region>.<id> The flow log's log group Flow Log OCID ocid1.log.oc1.<region>.<id> The VCN flow log to read

  5. Toggle Enabled to on

  6. Click Save

The three OCIDs together form the search scope: compartment, log group, log.

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Data Flow
docs.text:
After saving, verify the integration is working:

  1. Check connection status — The integration tile should show a green status indicator within 1–2 polling cycles

  2. Check Signal Client logs:

    docker logs signal-client-svc --tail=50 | grep -i "oci"

  3. Check artifacts in Analytics — Navigate to WitFoo Analytics Signals → Search and search for network flow artifacts from this source

docs.title: How Reading Works
docs.text:
• The connector reads the log in pages of up to 1,000 records and follows the API's page continuation, so a busy log is read to its end.
  • Flow records become searchable some time after the flow starts, so the connector reads 4 minutes behind the present.
  • If one instant of the log holds more than 10,000 records, the connector reads up to that limit, moves on, and logs a warning that names the instant.
  • It logs a warning when a polling cycle ends more than 5 minutes behind the log.

Long flows

An OCI flow that lasts longer than the connector's four-minute guard is never read. This is a known limit of this release.
