docs.title: Step 1: Create credentials in Google Cloud Platform
docs.text:
1. Open the Google Cloud Console and go to IAM & Admin → Service Accounts.
  2. Create a service account with read-only roles (see Required APIs and permissions below).
  3. Create a JSON key for the service account and download it.
  4. Note the Project ID to audit.

docs.title: Required APIs and permissions
docs.text:
Test Connection only needs resourcemanager.projects.get. A full audit run calls five Google APIs — each must be enabled on the audited project and the service account needs the matching read permission. A disabled API is the usual cause of a "Corporate login required" error (the request is rejected before authentication is evaluated).

Enable all required APIs in one command:

gcloud services enable \
  cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com iam.googleapis.com \
  storage.googleapis.com compute.googleapis.com sqladmin.googleapis.com \
  --project <PROJECT_ID>
Audit check Google API Service-account permission (role) Project access (Test Connection) cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com resourcemanager.projects.get (roles/browser or roles/viewer) Org-policy domain restriction cloudresourcemanager / orgpolicy.googleapis.com resourcemanager.projects.getIamPolicy, orgpolicy.policy.get (roles/iam.securityReviewer) Audit logging config cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com resourcemanager.projects.getIamPolicy (roles/iam.securityReviewer) Service-account key rotation iam.googleapis.com iam.serviceAccounts.list, iam.serviceAccountKeys.list (roles/iam.securityReviewer) Public buckets storage.googleapis.com storage.buckets.list, storage.buckets.getIamPolicy (roles/iam.securityReviewer + a list role) Default network compute.googleapis.com compute.networks.list (roles/compute.viewer) Cloud SQL SSL sqladmin.googleapis.com cloudsql.instances.list, cloudsql.instances.get (roles/cloudsql.viewer)

Simplest grant (covers all checks):

for ROLE in roles/iam.securityReviewer roles/cloudsql.viewer roles/compute.viewer roles/storage.objectViewer; do
  gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <PROJECT_ID> \
    --member="serviceAccount:<SA_EMAIL>" --role="$ROLE"
done

docs.title: Step 2: Configure in Analytics
docs.text:
1. Open Reporter → Auditor and select the Connectors tab.
  2. Click Add Connector and choose Google Cloud Platform.

  3. Fill in the connector form:

    Field Required Description Service Account JSON Yes Full JSON key file contents from step 1 Project ID Yes GCP project to audit

  4. Set the Schedule (default 0 */6 * * * — every 6 hours).

  5. Toggle Enabled on and click Save.

docs.title: Step 3: Validate
docs.text:

  2. Click Run Now (requires auditor:execute) to trigger an immediate audit.
  3. After the run completes, open the Findings tab — Google Cloud Platform findings appear with severity, evidence, framework mappings, and remediation guidance.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Authentication failed — confirm the JSON key is pasted in full and not expired.
  • Permission denied — ensure the service account has the roles in Required APIs and permissions.
  • Wrong project — verify the Project ID matches the project you intend to audit.
  • HTTP 404 on cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<id> — confirm the Project ID is correct and the service account has resourcemanager.projects.get (Browser/Viewer) on it. (The connector uses the per-service host; the legacy www.googleapis.com host returns 404 for every project.)
  • "Corporate login required" — a required Google API is not enabled on the project. Run the gcloud services enable … command above. If your org uses Context-Aware Access / VPC Service Controls, also confirm the service account is not excluded by an access-level policy.
  • "Cloud SQL requires SSL" — if shown as a finding (not an error), the check is working as designed: the instance requires SSL = compliant. If shown as a hard error during the run, enable sqladmin.googleapis.com and grant roles/cloudsql.viewer.

  3. Configure name, description, visibility (Public/Private), and indicator sources

docs.title: Publication Properties
docs.text: Field Description Name Publication title Status Active, Paused, or Draft Indicator count Published indicators Subscribers Organizations subscribed Visibility Public or Private

docs.title: What Gets Published
docs.text:
• Indicators from confirmed (true-positive) incidents
  • Nodes flagged as malicious during investigation
  • Manually added indicators

Review Before Publishing

Published indicators are shared externally. Do not include internal IPs or legitimate domains.

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text: Connect to external threat intelligence feeds via CyberGrid.

docs.title: Managing Subscriptions
docs.text:
1. Navigate to CyberGrid > Subscriptions
  2. Browse available feeds
  3. Click Subscribe and configure sync schedule
  4. Set confidence thresholds (optional)

docs.title: Subscription Properties
docs.text: Field Description Feed name Intelligence feed name Publisher Organization providing the feed Status Active, Paused, or Error Last sync Most recent successful sync Indicator count Indicators from this feed Sync schedule Update frequency

docs.title: Indicator Types
docs.text: Feeds can include IPs, domains, file hashes, URLs, and email addresses.

docs.title: Enrichment Integration
docs.text: Matched indicators update node threat scores, affecting incident severity and compliance calculations.

docs.title: Graph
docs.text: The Graph module visualizes the relationship network built from correlated security artifacts. As artifacts are ingested, the Graph Processor extracts entities (nodes) and identifies relationships (edges) between them, forming a queryable knowledge graph stored in Cassandra.

docs.title: How the Graph Works
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Artifact Ingested] --> GP[Graph Processor]
    GP --> N[Create/Update Nodes]
    GP --> E[Create/Update Edges]
    N --> C[(Cassandra)]
    E --> C
  1. Artifact ingestion — Security events arrive via the Artifact Ingestion service
  2. Entity extraction — The Graph Processor identifies entities: IP addresses, domains, users, hostnames, hashes
  3. Node creation — Each unique entity becomes a node with properties and classification flags
  4. Edge creation — Relationships between entities become edges with timestamps and metadata
  5. Correlation — The Dispatcher uses the graph to group related artifacts into incidents

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text: Nodes represent distinct entities observed in your security data. Each node has a type, value, and set of classification flags (managed, internal, trusted, infrastructure).

docs.title: Edges
docs.text: Edges represent observed relationships between nodes. Each edge records the relationship type, first/last seen timestamps, and the artifacts that created the relationship.

docs.title: Node Classification
docs.text:
Nodes are automatically classified using framework-based rules:

Flag Meaning Managed Entity is under your organization's management Internal Entity is within your network boundary Trusted Entity is known-good and trusted Infrastructure Entity is an infrastructure device (router, switch, firewall)

These flags are used by classification rules to determine incident severity and by compliance calculations for focus-based scoring.

docs.title: Edges
docs.text: Edges represent observed relationships between nodes in the knowledge graph. When the Graph Processor identifies that two entities appear together in an artifact, it creates or updates an edge recording that relationship.

docs.title: Edge Properties
docs.text: Property Description Source node The originating entity Target node The destination entity Relationship type Category of the connection First seen Timestamp of the earliest observation Last seen Timestamp of the most recent observation Artifact count Number of artifacts creating this relationship Weight Calculated significance based on frequency and recency

docs.title: Relationship Types
docs.text: Type Example Description communicated_with IP to IP Network communication observed resolved_to Domain to IP DNS resolution authenticated_as IP to User Authentication event accessed User to Hostname System access contains Hostname to Hash File observed on system associated_with Generic Artifact co-occurrence

docs.title: Browsing Edges
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Graph > Edges
  2. Filter by source/target node type or relationship type
  3. Use the time range selector to view edges within a specific window
  4. Click an edge to see the underlying artifacts

docs.title: Edge Detail
docs.text:
The edge detail view shows:

  • Source and target nodes with links to their detail pages
  • Timeline of observations (first seen through last seen)
  • Artifact list — All artifacts that contributed to this edge
  • Related incidents — Incidents that include artifacts from this edge

docs.title: Graph Traversal
docs.text: Edges enable graph traversal for incident investigation. Starting from any node, follow edges to discover related entities and understand the full scope of an incident. The correlation engine uses this traversal to automatically group related artifacts into incidents.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text: Nodes are the fundamental entities in the WitFoo Analytics knowledge graph. Each node represents a distinct object observed in your security data.

docs.title: Node Types
docs.text: Type Example Description IP 192.168.1.100 IPv4 or IPv6 address Domain example.com DNS domain name User jsmith User account identifier Hostname workstation-01 System hostname Hash a1b2c3... File hash (MD5, SHA1, SHA256) Email user@example.com Email address URL https://example.com/path Full URL

docs.title: Node Properties
docs.text:
Each node stores:

  • Value — The entity identifier (IP, domain, etc.)
  • Type — Entity type from the table above
  • First seen — Timestamp of earliest artifact referencing this node
  • Last seen — Timestamp of most recent artifact
  • Artifact count — Number of artifacts associated with this node
  • Frameworks — Compliance framework indices where this node appears
  • Flags — Classification flags (managed, internal, trusted, infrastructure)

docs.title: Classification Flags
docs.text:
Flag Purpose Managed Part of your managed infrastructure — counts toward compliance denominators Internal Inside your network boundary Trusted Known-good entity — reduces incident severity Infrastructure Network infrastructure device — used in infrastructure-focus compliance

Flags are set automatically by framework-based classification rules and can be manually overridden.

docs.title: Searching Nodes
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Graph > Nodes
  2. Enter a search term (IP, domain, username, etc.)
  3. Filter by node type, flags, or framework association
  4. Click a node to view its detail page

docs.title: Node Detail Page
docs.text:
The detail page shows:

  • Summary — Node value, type, flags, first/last seen
  • Edges — All relationships to other nodes
  • Artifacts — Artifacts that reference this node
  • Incidents — Incidents containing this node
  • Enrichments — GeoIP, DNS, WHOIS, threat intel data (when available)

docs.title: Framework Association
docs.text: Nodes are associated with compliance frameworks via integer indices. The indices are assigned by sorting enabled framework machine names alphabetically. This mapping is used by compliance calculations to count nodes per framework.

docs.title: Health
docs.text: Real-time monitoring of your WitFoo Analytics deployment.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: Real-time and historical metrics for all Docker containers. Auto-refreshes every 15 seconds.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: Configurable alert rules for container metrics and service availability.

docs.title: Dashboard Overview
docs.text:
• Service status cards — Clickable tiles showing container state with CPU/memory gauges
  • KPI tiles — Total containers, healthy count, average CPU/memory
  • Historical charts — Time-series resource usage (limited to 100 data points)

docs.title: Container States
docs.text: State Color Running Green Unhealthy Yellow Stopped Red Restarting Orange

docs.title: Auto-Refresh
docs.text: Updates every 15 seconds via silent background requests.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Action Required Permission View health data health:read Configure alerts health:manage View metrics metrics:read

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: Configurable notifications when container metrics exceed thresholds.

docs.title: Alert Types
docs.text: Type Triggers On CPU CPU exceeds threshold for duration Memory Memory exceeds threshold Disk Disk exceeds threshold Container State Container stops/unhealthy/restarting Restart Count Restarts exceed N in window

docs.title: Creating Alert Rules
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Health > Alerts
  2. Click Create Alert
  3. Select type, container, threshold, duration, severity
  4. Choose notification channels
  5. Click Save

The form adapts based on alert type — CPU/Memory/Disk show threshold/duration; Container State shows state selector; Restart Count shows count/window fields.

docs.title: Cooldown
docs.text: Default 15-minute cooldown per alert type + severity + container combination. Prevents notification spam during sustained issues.

docs.title: Notification Channels
docs.text:
Channel Format Email HTML with severity-colored header Slack Block Kit structured message Webhook JSON payload

Configure channels in Admin > Settings > Notifications.

docs.title: Alert History
docs.text: Retained for 30 days with timestamp, type, severity, container, metric value, and notification status.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: Detailed metrics for every Docker container in your deployment.

docs.title: Container List
docs.text:
Open Health > Containers. The page lists every container in a table with the columns Container Name, State, Health, CPU %, Memory %, Uptime and Restarts. Click a container to open its detail.

The page works on an appliance that has been running for a long time. A slow container-health read answers "service unavailable" promptly instead of an error after 30 seconds.

docs.title: Color-Coded Metrics
docs.text: Threshold Color < 70% Normal 70-90% Yellow > 90% Red

docs.title: Current Metrics
docs.text: Metric Source CPU % (cpuDelta / systemDelta) * numCPUs * 100 Memory RSS from Docker stats Network I/O Bytes received/transmitted Disk I/O Bytes read/written PIDs Process count

docs.title: Historical Charts
docs.text: Time-series bar charts stored in Cassandra using TimeUUID ordering.

docs.title: Core Services
docs.text: Container Service witfoo-analytics-cassandra Cassandra database witfoo-analytics-nats NATS message broker witfoo-analytics-incident-engine Core business logic witfoo-analytics-api API gateway witfoo-analytics-ui SvelteKit frontend witfoo-analytics-artifact-ingestion Artifact receiver witfoo-analytics-graph-processor Graph builder witfoo-analytics-dispatcher Event dispatcher witfoo-analytics-reverse-proxy Request router

docs.title: Down and Unhealthy Containers
docs.text:
A running container that Docker marks unhealthy counts as a down service. The Console shows its node as Error, and a critical cluster problem report is raised.

  • A container that was already unhealthy before the upgrade to 1.2.0 starts alerting once you upgrade. On WFA appliances this needs WFA 2.5.1 or later.
  • An exited or stopped container is not counted as a down service. Only a running container that fails its health check is.
  • The analytics Cassandra health check notices a node that has stopped serving clients, for example on a full data disk, instead of reading healthy while sign-ins fail.

docs.title: Licence Status
docs.text:
The Health page shows the licence's days remaining only for a licence it can read: active, expiring or expired.

When the last licence check failed, the page says "The last license check failed, so the license status shown may be out of date. The incident-engine log has the reason."

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Two columns are blank. The table leaves the Container Name and Uptime columns blank. State, health, CPU, memory and restarts are shown.
  • Empty after the upgrade. The page is empty for the first collection cycle, about 15 seconds, after the upgrade. Containers removed before the upgrade are no longer listed.
  • Cassandra on a CPU-starved appliance. On an appliance that is short of CPU, the Cassandra health check can time out for several minutes in a row. Cassandra then reads unhealthy and a problem report is raised, but nothing restarts it.

docs.title: Prometheus Integration
docs.text: Metrics exported at /api/v1/metrics with witfoo_container_* prefix.

docs.title: Observer
docs.text: The Observer module tracks analyst work and captures institutional knowledge about security operations. It provides structured workflows for documenting investigations, defining threat patterns, and recording observations.

docs.title: Work Units
docs.text: Individual tasks or investigation steps performed by analysts. Work units track time spent, status, and outcomes for each piece of security work.

docs.title: Work Collections
docs.text: Groups of related work units organized into logical investigations. Work collections aggregate time and effort across multiple tasks.

docs.title: MO Definitions
docs.text: Modus operandi (MO) definitions describe known attack patterns and threat behaviors. Analysts create MO definitions to codify institutional knowledge about recurring threats.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text: Freeform notes and findings recorded during investigations. Observations capture context that doesn't fit into structured fields — analyst insights, external research, and contextual notes.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
graph TD
    I[Incident Detected] --> WC[Create Work Collection]
    WC --> WU1[Work Unit: Triage]
    WC --> WU2[Work Unit: Investigation]
    WC --> WU3[Work Unit: Remediation]
    WU2 --> O[Record Observations]
    WU2 --> MO[Match/Create MO Definition]
  1. An incident triggers a new work collection
  2. Analysts create work units for each investigation step
  3. During investigation, analysts record observations and match to known MO definitions
  4. Work collection aggregates total effort for reporting

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Action Required Permission View observer data observer:read Create/edit work items observer:write Manage MO definitions observer:manage

docs.title: MO Definitions
docs.text: Modus operandi (MO) definitions capture known attack patterns, threat behaviors, and adversary techniques. They serve as institutional knowledge that helps analysts recognize recurring threats and respond consistently.

docs.title: MO Properties
docs.text: Field Description Name Pattern identifier Description Detailed description of the attack pattern or behavior Category Classification (malware, phishing, lateral movement, etc.) Indicators Observable indicators associated with this MO TTPs Tactics, techniques, and procedures Severity Typical severity when this MO is observed Response playbook Recommended response steps Created by Analyst who defined the MO

docs.title: Creating MO Definitions
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Observer > MO Definitions
  2. Click Create MO Definition
  3. Fill in the name, description, and category
  4. Add indicators and TTPs
  5. Document the recommended response
  6. Click Save

docs.title: Using MO Definitions
docs.text:
During incident investigation, analysts can:

  • Match incidents to MOs — Link an incident to a known MO definition
  • Create new MOs — Document newly observed patterns for future reference
  • Search by indicators — Find MOs matching observed indicators in current data

docs.title: Categories
docs.text: Category Examples Malware Ransomware, trojan, worm, rootkit Phishing Spear phishing, credential harvesting, BEC Lateral Movement Pass-the-hash, RDP abuse, SMB pivoting Exfiltration DNS tunneling, cloud storage abuse, encrypted channels Persistence Scheduled tasks, registry modification, backdoor accounts

docs.title: Relationship to Observations
docs.text: MO definitions provide structure while observations capture freeform context. An investigation typically involves linking an incident to an MO definition and recording specific observations about how the pattern manifested in that case.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text: Observations are freeform notes and findings recorded during security investigations. They capture analyst insights, external research, and contextual information that complements the structured data in work units and MO definitions.

docs.title: Observation Properties
docs.text: Field Description Title Brief summary of the observation Content Detailed findings (supports markdown) Author Analyst who recorded the observation Related incident Associated incident (optional) Related work unit Associated work unit (optional) Tags Freeform labels for categorization Timestamp When the observation was recorded

docs.title: Creating Observations
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Observer > Observations
  2. Click Create Observation
  3. Enter a title and detailed content
  4. Optionally link to an incident or work unit
  5. Add relevant tags
  6. Click Save

Observations can also be created from the incident detail page or work unit detail page for quick contextual notes.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Investigation notes — Document findings during incident analysis
  • External intelligence — Record relevant information from external sources
  • Analyst handoff — Leave context for the next shift or team member
  • Lessons learned — Post-incident notes for future reference
  • Evidence documentation — Capture screenshots, logs, or analysis results

docs.title: Search and Filter
docs.text:
Search observations by:

  • Text content (full-text search)
  • Author
  • Tags
  • Date range
  • Associated incident or work unit

docs.title: Relationship to Other Observer Components
docs.text:
Observations complement the structured data in the Observer module:

  • Work units track what was done and how long it took
  • Work collections group related work
  • MO definitions describe known patterns
  • Observations capture everything else — the human context that makes investigations meaningful

docs.title: Work Collections
docs.text: Work collections group related work units into logical investigations. They provide a high-level view of effort spent on a security incident or ongoing investigation.

docs.title: Work Collection Properties
docs.text: Field Description Name Collection title Description Purpose and scope of the investigation Status Active, Complete, or Archived Owner Lead analyst for the collection Work units List of associated work units Total time Aggregated time from all work units Related incidents Linked incidents Created/Updated Timestamps

docs.title: Creating Collections
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Observer > Work Collections
  2. Click Create Collection
  3. Enter a name and description
  4. Assign an owner
  5. Click Save

Add work units to a collection from either the collection detail page or when creating/editing individual work units.

docs.title: How Long Collections Are Kept
docs.text: Work collections and their notes do not expire. A collection's audit log is kept for 90 days.

docs.title: Deleting a Collection
docs.text:
Deleting a work collection also deletes its members, assignments, tasks, notes and the notes' files. Deleting a task does the same for what belongs to the task.

A delete that fails keeps the collection or task, so you can repeat it.

docs.title: Updating a Collection Through the API
docs.text:
POST and PUT on /api/v1/work-collections change only what the request states:

  • Every member (name, description, criteria or criteria_json, enabled, assigned_to, status_id) is optional.
  • A member the body leaves out, or sets to null, keeps its stored value. A member it states, empty included, replaces it.
  • An update writes only what it states, so it never overwrites the collection's statistics.
  • A collection created without enabled is stored disabled.
  • A request that states nothing, that states both criteria and criteria_json, or whose collection does not validate is refused with HTTP 400.

See Incidents API.

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
Work collections automatically aggregate metrics from their child work units:

  • Total time — Sum of all work unit time entries
  • Status breakdown — Count of open, in-progress, and complete units
  • Priority distribution — Mix of priority levels across units

These aggregates flow into the Reporter module for cost and efficiency analysis.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Collection Scope Incident response All work units related to a single incident Threat hunt Proactive investigation across multiple data sources Compliance audit Evidence gathering for a specific framework Recurring task Ongoing operational tasks (weekly review, etc.)

docs.title: Work Units
docs.text: Work units represent individual tasks or investigation steps performed by security analysts. Each work unit tracks what was done, who did it, and how long it took.

docs.title: Work Unit Properties
docs.text: Field Description Title Short description of the task Description Detailed explanation of work performed Assignee Analyst responsible for the work Status Current state (New, Investigating, Resolved, Closed, Disrupted) Priority Task priority (Low, Medium, High, Critical) Time spent Hours invested in this task Related incident Link to the associated incident (optional) Work collection Parent collection grouping related units Created/Updated Timestamps for tracking

docs.title: Creating Work Units
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Observer > Work Units
  2. Click Create Work Unit
  3. Fill in the title, description, and assignee
  4. Optionally link to an incident or work collection
  5. Click Save

Work units can also be created directly from an incident detail page.

docs.title: Triage Summary
docs.text:
The detail page opens on a triage summary. The header shows:

  • the work unit's name, its status and its suspicion verdict;
  • a severity band and its MO tag;
  • a scope line that counts its artifacts, nodes, users and IP addresses.

The response actions stay in a bar that is visible on every tab: AI summary, share to chat, share to CyberGrid, refresh, Add to Collection, update status, and Replay.

The identifiers, dates and score breakdown are in a Details section that starts closed. The score breakdown shows the component weights (Node Score, MO Coverage, Alarm Density, Entity Diversity) and an outlier warning when a score was dampened.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Tab Contents Graph Interactive graph of the work unit's nodes and edges Evidence Sections for the work unit's Nodes, Edges and a Map of where its nodes are Artifacts The work unit's artifacts, as a histogram, a table and a timeline Activity Notes and the audit log Response Tasks and playbooks. The tab shows the number of open tasks.

Each tab loads the first time you open it and then stays loaded. The page reads the work unit's artifacts once, and the histogram, the table and the timeline share that set. The open-task count on the Response tab appears when that tab is first opened.

When the Response tab's read fails, it is tried once and offers Retry.

docs.title: Edge and Signal Details
docs.text:
The edge window opens on the relationship: a sentence that names both ends over the edge type, the observed time span with the number of observations and, when there are enough observations, a small sparkline. Below it are the evidence (bytes, protocols and the matched rules), the two endpoints (select one to open its node) and the observed signals. Editing and the raw fields are in an Advanced section.

The signal window opens on the event: a sentence of who did what to whom, its time, its severity verdict (critical, high, medium or low, shown with the vendor's own label) and the ATT&CK techniques it matched, by name. Below it are what happened, who and where, and why it matters.

docs.title: Node Relationship Graph
docs.text:
In a node's detail, the relationship graph grows on request:

  1. It opens with the node's top-ranked relationships.
  2. Show 5 more adds the next five without moving what is already on screen. A line reads "Showing X of Y relationships".
  3. Undo removes the last batch, and Reset graph returns to the first view.

The graph stops growing at 200 nodes and says so.

docs.title: Replay
docs.text:
Replay rebuilds a work unit in the order it was observed. Open it with Replay in the response bar, or Replay timeline beside the graph.

  • Nodes and edges appear as time advances, the artifacts stream into a list at the side, and the MITRE techniques seen so far gather under their tactics.
  • Play, pause, previous and next event, a playback speed and a draggable timeline control it. The elapsed-time readout accepts a typed time.
  • The replay shows at most 600 nodes. It says "Replaying top N of M nodes" when it leaves some out.
  • Escape closes a detail window opened over the replay, or cancels an edit of the elapsed time. Escape with nothing open leaves the replay.

Replay opens only for a role that can read it.

Escape key

Holding Escape down closes an open detail window and then leaves the replay. Press Escape once for each window.

docs.title: Status Workflow
docs.text: ID Status 1 New 2 Investigating 3 Resolved 4 Closed 5 Disrupted

docs.title: Time Tracking
docs.text:
Time spent on work units feeds into the Reporter module's cost/savings analysis. The total investigation time across all work units contributes to:

  • FTE calculations — How many full-time analysts are needed
  • Cost per incident — Average cost based on analyst hourly rates
  • Savings analysis — Time saved through automation vs manual investigation

docs.title: Filtering and Search
docs.text:
The Work Units list shows the node data it holds: its Countries column, Geo Heatmap and Graph views, and its Node Type, Location and Country filters are filled.

  • Searches on Node IP, Node Hostname, Node Type, Node MAC, Node Username, Node Internal and Node Managed return the matching work units.
  • The Status facet lists the work units in any of the statuses you tick. The suspicion level filter works the same way.
  • A link to Work Units (from a node's details, the ATT&CK page or a status link) applies the filters it carries, ahead of any filters the search bar remembers.
  • The list shows the result of your latest filter or page change, even when an earlier request finishes last.

When a list with more than one status is read over only the newest 10,000 work units, the page says: "This list covers only your organization's newest work units, so older work units with the selected statuses are not shown."

docs.title: Removed Search Fields
docs.text:
The Work Units search offers only fields the list can answer. These fields are removed: Edges, Edge Type, Edge Label, Stream Name, Message, Artifact Severity, Server IP and Action, and the Filter by Alarm Rule... dropdown.

A saved search or link that still names one lists work units without that filter and shows a notice: "These filters were not applied, because this list cannot filter on them: …"

The time range on the Work Units page is labelled Time range for CyberGrid jobs:. It sets only the window of the CyberGrid jobs created from the page. The list itself is not limited by time.

Known limitation

A node, ATT&CK technique or Client IP filter reads only that item's newest work units, up to the page size, and the total counts only those.

docs.title: Reporter
docs.text: The Reporter module generates executive-level reports on your security operations posture. It combines data from incidents, compliance frameworks, security products, and business settings.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: High-level KPIs including incident counts, true positive/false positive ratios, mean time to detect, and mean time to respond.

docs.title: Compliance Readiness
docs.text: Framework-by-framework compliance scoring with per-control drill-down, focus-based filtering, and delta indicators.

docs.title: Tool Effectiveness
docs.text: Sankey flow diagrams showing artifact-to-incident pipelines, Venn diagrams of product coverage overlap, and per-product detection metrics.

docs.title: Cost & Savings
docs.text: FTE analysis, profit & loss table, savings histograms, and security spend as a percentage of revenue.

docs.title: Audit Report
docs.text: Organization-wide configuration-audit snapshot: overall and per-framework compliance, findings by severity, per-connector results, top failing checks, and a 30-day trend. Connectors are configured in the Auditor section.

docs.title: Date Range Selection
docs.text: All reports are filtered by date range. Click the date tag in the report header to open the date range picker. Select from preset ranges (7 days, 30 days, 90 days, 1 year) or choose custom dates.

docs.title: CSV Export
docs.text: Each report section supports CSV export. Click the Download button to export data. Filenames include report type and current date.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Action Required Permission View reports reports:read Export reports reports:write Configure settings reports:manage

docs.title: Business Settings Dependency
docs.text: Reporter calculations depend on settings in Admin > Settings > Business Metrics. See Business Metrics.

docs.title: Audit Report
docs.text: The Audit Report is the organization-wide snapshot view of the Auditor. It summarizes the latest configuration-audit results across every connector and compliance framework.

docs.title: What the report shows
docs.text:
• Overall compliance — the org-wide pass rate, plus total checks, passes, and failures.
  • Findings by severity — failing findings grouped by critical, high, medium, low, and info.
  • Framework coverage — per-framework compliance cards and a gauge for the selected framework.
  • Per-connector results — pass/fail rollups for each configured platform.
  • Top failing checks — the ten highest-severity failing checks, each with a remediation summary and a View findings link into the live Auditor.
  • 30-day trend — a daily compliance trend line.

docs.title: Date range
docs.text: The report is snapshot-based and uses the same date-range picker as the other Reporter pages. Click the date tag in the header to choose a preset or custom range.

docs.title: AI Analysis
docs.text: The AI Analysis button generates an on-demand natural-language summary of the report. Audit snapshots are not summarized automatically — analysis runs only when you request it.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
• CSV — the Download button exports the top failing checks and framework rollups. Filenames include the current date.
  • Print — the Print / Save as PDF button uses the browser print dialog with print styling. There is no separate PDF export.

docs.title: Drill-down and cross-links
docs.text: Full findings are not embedded in the snapshot. Use Open live Auditor (or the View findings links) to drill into the live Auditor, where findings load on demand. The Compliance Readiness report also links from individual controls to their backing audit findings.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Action Required Permission View the Audit Report reports:read Drill into findings (live Auditor) auditor:read

docs.title: Compliance Readiness
docs.text: The Compliance Readiness report shows your organization's compliance posture against enabled security frameworks using focus-based scoring.

docs.title: Framework Selection
docs.text: Select a framework from the dropdown. The primary framework is selected by default.

docs.title: Compliance Score
docs.text:
Overall score displayed as a gauge chart:

Score Range Color Status > 75% Green Compliant > 0% Yellow Partial 0% Red Unmet

docs.title: Focus-Based Scoring
docs.text:
Each control has a focus type determining the compliance denominator:

Focus Denominator Computer Managed nodes User User nodes Infrastructure Device Infrastructure nodes Product Security products

Score = (green + yellow nodes) / auto-detectable nodes * 100. Manual-only controls excluded.

docs.title: Per-Control Table
docs.text: Column Description Control ID Framework control identifier Control Name Human-readable name Focus Type (Computer=blue, User=purple, Infra=magenta, Product=green) Compliance % Calculated percentage Detection Product + confidence (e.g., "Palo Alto (95%)") Status Compliant / Partial / Unmet / Manual / N/A. N/A means no node is in the control's scope.

docs.title: Capability provider
docs.text: A control that WitFoo Analytics performs for the whole estate lists WitFoo Analytics in the Detection column with the note performs this control, and no coverage percentage. Hover the note for the full explanation: the Coverage figure on that row counts hosts running a contributing third-party sensor and is not a measure of the platform's own reach. For System Component Inventory, the inventory is a rolling 7-day observation of what has been seen, not a configuration management database.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Two combinable filter dimensions: Compliance status and Focus type. An N/A status filter appears when at least one control is N/A.

When you change the date range while an earlier request is still loading, the table shows the answer for the range you selected last.

docs.title: Audit Findings
docs.text: Control rows backed by Auditor checks show an Audit findings (N) link in the actions column, where N is the number of failing audit checks for that control. The link opens the Auditor Findings tab pre-filtered to that framework and control, so you can see and remediate the exact failing checks. It appears only when there are failing findings, independent of whether a detection product is deployed for the control.

docs.title: Delta Indicator
docs.text: Shows compliance score change across date range snapshots.

docs.title: CSV Export
docs.text: Exports per-control table with current filters. An N/A control reads N/A in the CSV. Filename: {framework}_Compliance_{date}.csv, with spaces in the framework name replaced by _.

docs.title: Cost & Savings
docs.text: Financial analysis of security operations including FTE requirements and automation savings.

docs.title: Cost & Savings Waterfall
docs.text:
The Cost & Savings Waterfall shows how gross protection value nets against security costs. Each savings driver rises, each cost falls, and the net equals savings minus costs.

Step Kind Prevented Revenue Loss Savings Prevented Brand Damage Savings Prevented Legal Costs Savings IT Labor Savings Savings Insurance Coverage Savings Total Protection Subtotal Security Spend Cost False Positive Cost Cost Net Savings Result

Use View as table to read the same steps as a table. When the date range holds no cost or savings, the chart says "No cost or savings in range".

docs.title: FTE Analysis
docs.text:
A summary line states the calculated analyst headcount against the budgeted headcount, as a surplus or a deficit. The page has no FTE gauge.

FTE Needed = (Total Incidents * Avg Hours per Incident) / 2,080

Avg Hours = Investigation Time + Restore Time (default: 2.25 hours). 2,080 = 40 hrs/week * 52 weeks.

docs.title: Profit & Loss Summary
docs.text:
Financial summary in monospace format (IBM Plex Mono):

Section Contents Revenue Annual revenue Security Spend Annual security budget Product Costs Sum of product costs Personnel Costs FTE count * analyst salary Net Position Revenue impact

docs.title: Security Spend Ratio
docs.text: Security Spend % = (Annual Security Spend / Annual Revenue) * 100

docs.title: Savings by Category
docs.text:
Bar chart showing the cost savings by category.

Percentages are rounded as your browser formats numbers, so -15.45 shows as -15.5%.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: The Executive Summary provides high-level KPIs for security operations leadership.

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: Metric Description Calculation Total Incidents Incidents in the date range Count of all incidents True Positives Confirmed security incidents Status: Disrupted (5) or Resolved (3) False Positives Non-incidents Status: Closed (4) TP/FP Ratio Classification accuracy True positives / false positives MTTD Mean time to detect Avg time from first artifact to incident creation MTTR Mean time to respond Avg time from creation to resolution

docs.title: Page Layout
docs.text:
The Executive Summary page leads with key figures and has no gauges.

  1. Key figures — WitFoo Readiness, Return on Investment, FTE Headcount, FTE Ratio and Compliance, as large-format figures
  2. Attainment vs Target — Key figures against their targets
  3. Executive Trends (Daily) — Daily WitFoo Readiness, ROI and CSC compliance percentages across the selected window
  4. Investigation Snapshot — MTTD/MTTR metrics, closure rates, and analyst workload
  5. Daily Incident Summary — Incidents per day by status. Click a bar to drill into the underlying work units.
  6. Analyst Workload — Per-analyst incident assignments and resolution metrics
  7. Vulnerability Summary — Host vulnerability scan results from graph node analysis

FTE Ratio is FTE Needed ÷ FTE Budgeted × 100. Lower is better: at or below 100% means budgeted staff can cover the workload.

Percentages are rounded as your browser formats numbers, so -15.45 shows as -15.5%.

docs.title: True Positive Classification
docs.text:
TP/FP classification uses incident status IDs:

  • True Positive: Status is disrupted (5) or resolved (3)
  • False Positive: Status is closed (4)

docs.title: Trend Indicators
docs.text: Each KPI shows a trend arrow comparing the current period to the previous period of equal length.

docs.title: Tool Effectiveness
docs.text: Analyzes how security products contribute to incident detection and response.

docs.title: Sankey Flow Diagram
docs.text:
Shows artifact flows from products through types to incident severities. Products ranked by artifact count, top-N shown individually, remainder as "Other".

The Incident Flow chart draws only the flows the report holds. A tool that has incidents but no flow data is named in a note under the chart and is not drawn.

docs.title: Product Coverage Venn
docs.text:
Overlap between security products. 1-4 products use fixed geometric layouts; 5-8 use radial layout.

The Product Incident Overlap diagram draws the incident counts, exclusive counts and overlaps computed from each product's incidents, with no estimates. A report without them shows the Likely True+ Incidents diagram when it has data.

docs.title: Product Metrics Table
docs.text:
Column Description Product Security product name Artifacts Total artifacts generated Incidents Incidents from this product TP Rate True positive rate Coverage Compliance controls detected Cost Annual product cost Cost per Incident Product cost / incidents

Help tooltips explain calculations. Chart toolbars disabled for clean presentation.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text: The Signals module is your primary interface for investigating security data flowing through WitFoo Analytics. Every log line, alert, and event ingested by the platform becomes a signal -- a searchable artifact enriched with context, classified by type, and evaluated against your lead rules.

docs.title: What Are Signals?
docs.text:
Signals are normalized security artifacts collected from your environment. Each signal contains:

  • Raw data -- the original log entry or alert payload
  • Metadata -- timestamps, source IP, destination IP, hostname, user, and other extracted fields
  • Classification -- the artifact stream (IDS, authentication, firewall, DNS, endpoint, etc.)
  • Severity -- a normalized severity level from informational to critical
  • Enrichment -- additional context added by enrichment sources such as GeoIP location and threat intelligence feeds

When data enters the ingestion pipeline, WitFoo Analytics parses, normalizes, and stores it. Classification rules assign each artifact to a stream, enrichment sources add context, and lead rules evaluate whether the artifact warrants further investigation.

docs.title: Module Layout
docs.text:
The Signals section of the navigation contains the following pages:

Page Purpose Search Query and filter artifacts with full-text search, date ranges, and field filters Lead Rules Define rules that flag artifacts as potential leads for investigation Classification Rules Manage rules that assign artifacts to streams (IDS, auth, firewall, etc.) Enrichment Settings Configure external data sources that add context to artifacts

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
1. Search for artifacts matching a time window, severity, or keyword
  2. Review results and drill into individual signal details
  3. Identify patterns that should trigger future leads by creating lead rules
  4. Fine-tune how artifacts are categorized using classification rules
  5. Add external context by enabling enrichment sources

Start with Search

Most analysts begin their day in the Search page. Use saved searches to quickly revisit common queries, and export results when you need to share findings with your team.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Access to the Signals module requires the signals:read permission. Creating and editing rules requires signals:write. Your administrator assigns these permissions through role-based access control in the Admin section.

Data Retention

The volume of signals stored depends on your organization's retention settings. Administrators can configure retention periods in Admin > Settings > Business Metrics. Older signals are automatically purged when the retention window expires.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
Streams -- Logical groupings of artifacts by source type. Common streams include IDS alerts, authentication events, firewall logs, DNS queries, and endpoint telemetry. Classification rules determine which stream an artifact belongs to.

Leads -- Artifacts that match a lead rule are flagged for analyst attention. A lead indicates that an artifact has characteristics worth investigating, such as a connection to a known malicious IP or an unusual authentication pattern.

Enrichment -- The process of augmenting raw artifact data with external context. GeoIP enrichment adds geographic location to IP addresses. Threat intelligence enrichment cross-references indicators against known threat feeds.

Severity Levels -- Each artifact carries a severity from informational through critical. Severity is determined during ingestion based on the source data and any matching classification rules.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Search Artifacts -- Learn the search syntax and filtering options
  • Lead Rules -- Create rules that surface important artifacts
  • Classification Rules -- Control how artifacts are categorized
  • Enrichment Settings -- Add context from external sources

docs.title: Classification Rules
docs.text: Classification rules automatically assign severity and status to incidents based on matching criteria. They run after lead rules create incidents, evaluating node properties, artifact types, and graph relationships.

docs.title: How Classification Works
docs.text:
When an incident is created or updated, the classification engine evaluates all enabled rules in priority order. The first matching rule sets the incident's severity and status.

graph LR
    I[Incident Created] --> E[Evaluate Rules]
    E --> M{Match Found?}
    M -->|Yes| A[Apply Severity + Status]
    M -->|No| D[Keep Default]

docs.title: Rule Properties
docs.text: Field Description Name Human-readable rule identifier Priority Evaluation order (lower = higher priority) Enabled Whether the rule is active Severity Severity to assign on match (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Info) Status Status to assign on match Target Infrastructure When enabled, rule only matches infrastructure-flagged nodes

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
Rules can match on:

  • Node types — IP addresses, domains, users, hostnames
  • Node flags — Managed, internal, trusted, infrastructure
  • Artifact sources — Specific security products or log sources
  • Framework controls — Nodes associated with specific compliance controls
  • Lead rule matches — Incidents created by specific lead rules

docs.title: Managing Rules
docs.text: The Classification Rules page provides full CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations through a dedicated management interface.

docs.title: Create a Rule
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Signals > Classification Rules
  2. Click Create Rule
  3. Configure the matching conditions and assignment values
  4. Set the priority relative to existing rules
  5. Click Save

docs.title: Edit or Disable
docs.text: Click a rule in the table to edit its properties. Toggle the Enabled switch to activate or deactivate a rule without deleting it.

docs.title: Delete a Rule
docs.text:
Select a rule and click Delete to permanently remove it. Deletion does not retroactively change incidents that were previously classified by the rule.

Rule Priority

Rules evaluate in priority order. Place more specific rules at higher priority (lower number) than general catch-all rules.

docs.title: Rule Criteria Syntax
docs.text:
Rule conditions use a criteria expression format with field-operator-value triples:

Operator Description Example eq Equals node_type eq "ip_address" ne Not equals status_id ne 5 gte Greater than or equal suspicion_score gte 0.50 lte Less than or equal priority lte 2 contains String contains source contains "firewall" in Value in list node_type in ["ip_address", "domain"]

Multiple conditions are combined with AND logic -- all conditions must match for the rule to apply.

docs.title: How Rules Are Applied
docs.text:
Classification rules run automatically when signals are ingested and processed:

  1. Ingestion — New artifacts arrive via the artifact-ingestion service
  2. Lead rule evaluation — Lead rules fire to create or update incidents
  3. Classification — Enabled classification rules evaluate in priority order against the resulting incident
  4. Assignment — The first matching rule sets the severity and status

Rules are re-evaluated when incident properties change (e.g., new artifacts are added or graph relationships update).

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Action Required Permission View rules signals:read Create/edit rules signals:write Delete rules signals:manage

docs.title: Enrichment Settings
docs.text: Enrichment settings control how WitFoo Analytics augments artifacts and nodes with additional context during processing. Enrichments add metadata such as geolocation, DNS resolution, WHOIS data, and threat intelligence scoring.

docs.title: Enrichment Types
docs.text: Type Description Applied To GeoIP Geographic location lookup for IP addresses IP nodes DNS Reverse DNS and forward resolution IP and domain nodes WHOIS Domain registration and ownership data Domain nodes Threat Intel Reputation scoring from CyberGrid feeds IP, domain, hash nodes ASN Autonomous System Number lookup IP nodes

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Navigate to Search > Node Enrichment to manage enrichment configuration. The page is headed Node Enrichment Settings and needs the signals:manage permission.

docs.title: Enable or Disable Enrichments
docs.text: Each enrichment type can be independently enabled or disabled. Disabled enrichments are skipped during artifact processing.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
External enrichment sources have configurable rate limits to prevent API throttling:

Setting Default Description Max requests per minute 60 Throttle for external API calls Cache TTL 24 hours How long enrichment results are cached Retry on failure 3 Number of retry attempts for failed lookups

docs.title: Viewing Enrichment Data
docs.text:
Enrichment results appear on node detail pages in the Enrichment tab. Each enrichment shows:

  • Source name and type
  • Timestamp of last enrichment
  • Raw enrichment data
  • Confidence score (when available)

docs.title: Vrax Threat Intelligence
docs.text: The Node Enrichment page also holds the Vrax threat intelligence and Vrax feed (MISP) cards. They import the reports your Vrax account holds and show them in a node's detail window. See Vrax Threat Intelligence.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Action Required Permission View settings signals:read Modify settings signals:manage

Upgrading to 1.2.0

From 1.2.0 the enrichment settings API (/api/v1/enrichment-settings) checks signals:read to read and signals:manage to change, on every request. Admin and Platform Admin are unchanged, and Analyst and ReadOnly can still read. Give signals:manage to any custom role that should change enrichment settings.

A request that turns an enrichment setting on or off must state the value, for example {"enabled": false}. An empty body is refused with HTTP 400.

docs.title: Lead Rules
docs.text: Lead rules automatically flag artifacts that match specified criteria, surfacing them as potential leads for analyst investigation. Rather than manually searching for patterns, you define the conditions once and let WitFoo Analytics continuously evaluate incoming data against your rules.

docs.title: What Is a Lead?
docs.text: A lead is an artifact that has been flagged by one or more lead rules as potentially significant. When an artifact matches a lead rule, it is marked as a lead and becomes visible in lead-focused views throughout the platform. Leads feed into the incident analysis pipeline, where they may contribute to the creation or escalation of incidents.

docs.title: Accessing Lead Rules
docs.text:
Navigate to Signals > Lead Rules from the main navigation. This page displays a table of all configured lead rules for your organization.

Required Permission

Viewing lead rules requires signals:read. Creating or editing lead rules requires signals:write.

docs.title: Lead Rules Table
docs.text:
The lead rules table shows all existing rules with the following columns:

Column Description Name A descriptive name for the rule Description A brief summary of what the rule detects Stream Which artifact stream the rule applies to (IDS, auth, firewall, etc.) Severity The severity level assigned to matching leads Status Whether the rule is enabled or disabled Match Count The number of artifacts that have matched this rule Last Match Timestamp of the most recent match

docs.title: Creating a Lead Rule
docs.text:
1. Click the Create Rule button in the toolbar
  2. Fill in the rule definition form:
    • Name -- A clear, descriptive name (e.g., "Brute Force SSH Attempts")
    • Description -- What the rule is designed to detect
    • Stream -- Select the artifact stream to evaluate (or "All" for cross-stream rules)
    • Severity -- The severity level to assign when matched (informational, low, medium, high, critical)
    • Conditions -- Define the matching criteria (see below)
  3. Click Save to create the rule in an enabled state

docs.title: Defining Conditions
docs.text:
Conditions specify which artifact fields to evaluate and what values to match. Each condition consists of:

  • Field -- The artifact field to inspect (e.g., src_ip, dst_ip, hostname, user)
  • Operator -- How to compare the field value (equals, contains, starts with, regex)
  • Value -- The target value to match against

You can add multiple conditions to a single rule. All conditions must match for the rule to trigger (AND logic).

Use Regex for Complex Patterns

The regex operator supports regular expressions for advanced pattern matching. For example, use user:admin.* to match any username starting with "admin".

docs.title: Editing a Lead Rule
docs.text:
1. Click on a rule row in the table to open the edit form
  2. Modify the fields you want to change
  3. Click Save to apply your changes

Changes take effect immediately. Existing artifacts are not retroactively re-evaluated, but all new incoming artifacts will be checked against the updated rule.

docs.title: Enabling and Disabling Rules
docs.text:
Toggle a rule's status to temporarily disable it without deleting the configuration:

  1. Click on the rule to open the edit form
  2. Toggle the Enabled switch
  3. Click Save

Disabled rules are shown with a dimmed appearance in the table and do not evaluate incoming artifacts.

Disabling vs. Deleting

Disable a rule when you want to temporarily stop it. Delete a rule only when you are certain it is no longer needed. Deleted rules cannot be recovered.

docs.title: Deleting a Lead Rule
docs.text:
1. Click on the rule to open the edit form
  2. Click the Delete button
  3. Confirm the deletion in the dialog

docs.title: How Lead Rules Are Evaluated
docs.text:
When an artifact is ingested:

  1. The artifact is classified into a stream by classification rules
  2. All enabled lead rules for that stream (and any "All" stream rules) are evaluated
  3. If the artifact's fields satisfy all conditions of a rule, the artifact is marked as a lead
  4. The lead is tagged with the rule name and assigned the rule's severity
  5. Leads flow into the incident analysis pipeline for correlation

Multiple rules can match the same artifact. In this case, the artifact carries all matching lead tags and the highest matched severity applies.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Name rules clearly -- Use names that describe the threat or behavior being detected, such as "Lateral Movement via RDP" or "DNS Tunneling Indicators"
  • Start broad, then narrow -- Begin with simple conditions and refine as you observe match volumes
  • Monitor match counts -- A rule with zero matches may have overly restrictive conditions; a rule with thousands of matches may need tightening
  • Use severity wisely -- Reserve critical and high severity for rules that detect confirmed threats or policy violations
  • Review regularly -- Periodically audit your lead rules to retire stale rules and add new ones based on emerging threats

docs.title: Relationship to Incidents
docs.text:
Leads generated by lead rules feed into the incident analysis engine. When multiple leads correlate around the same entities (IPs, users, hosts), the system may group them into an incident. The lead rule's severity influences the incident's overall severity assessment.

See the Observer module for how leads connect to work units and investigations.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: The Search page is the primary investigation tool in WitFoo Analytics. Use it to query artifacts across your entire data set, apply filters, visualize geographic distribution, and export results for further analysis.

docs.title: Accessing Search
docs.text: Navigate to Search > Signals from the main navigation bar. The page loads with a default time range showing recent artifacts. It needs the signals:read permission.

docs.title: The Search Interface
docs.text:
The Search page is organized into several areas:

  • Search bar -- Enter keywords and field filters, with autocomplete suggestions
  • Time range picker -- Select a predefined range or set a custom absolute date range
  • Filter bar -- Active filters displayed as removable tags below the search bar
  • Timeline -- A histogram of the matching events over the time range
  • Facets -- Counts of the matching events by field, for quick filtering
  • Results table -- Paginated list of matching artifacts with configurable columns
  • Detail panel -- Click anywhere in a row to inspect the full artifact, view its graph relationships, and take action

docs.title: Basic Search
docs.text: Type a word into the search bar and press Enter. A word typed without a field name matches events whose message contains it, ignoring upper and lower case. A phrase with spaces is matched as one piece of text. The word must be at least three bytes long.

docs.title: Field-Specific Search
docs.text:
Narrow your query by targeting specific fields with an operator:

Operator Meaning Example = Equals stream_name=ids != Does not equal action!=allowed : Contains user_name:admin >, >=, <, <= Comparison, on a number field only server_port>=1024

Comparisons work on number fields such as client port, server port, bytes sent, bytes received, duration and file size. Contains works on text fields only.

docs.title: Client and Server Fields
docs.text:
Most events have a client side and a server side.

You type Matches ip=, port=, hostname= Both sides at once: an event matches only when its client side and its server side both have that value client_ip=, server_ip=, client_port=, server_port=, client_hostname=, server_hostname= One side only

client_ip= and server_ip= accept an IPv4 or an IPv6 address.

docs.title: Combining Filters
docs.text:
Apply multiple filters simultaneously to narrow results. Each active filter appears as a tag in the filter bar. Remove a filter by clicking the close icon on its tag.

Filter Stacking

Filters are combined with AND logic. Adding a severity filter of "high" and a stream filter of "authentication" returns only high-severity authentication artifacts.

docs.title: Filters Apply to the Whole Range
docs.text: Every filter in the search bar, including contains, not-equal, comparisons, Client IP and Server IP matches, the Location filter and a free word, applies to the whole time range. It narrows the result list, the timeline and the facet counts, and every later page of results uses the same filters.

docs.title: When a Search Is Not Accepted
docs.text:
A filter the search cannot apply as typed is refused with the notice "The search was not accepted as typed. Check the filters and the search word, then try again." For example:

  • a comparison on a text field;
  • a contains on a number field;
  • a value that is not a number where a number is needed;
  • a word shorter than three bytes;
  • a page deeper than the first 10,000 results.

A refusal for permission reads "You do not have permission to run this search." Neither offers Retry.

docs.title: Time Range Selection
docs.text:
Click the time range picker to choose from preset windows or define a custom range.

Custom Range: Select "Custom" to pick specific start and end dates using the date picker calendar.

docs.title: How Far Back You Can Search
docs.text:
A search can cover up to your organization's search window. The window equals the Retention > Search setting. When that is not set, it is 30 days.

A wider range is refused: "That time range is too wide. Searches are limited to {limit} — narrow the range and try again."

docs.title: When a Search Reads Only Part of the Range
docs.text:
A filter such as contains, not-equal or a word is applied while the server reads the events, newest first. Such a read is bounded, and the result list, the timeline and the filtered facet counts each stop after 10 seconds.

When a search did not read the whole range, the page says so:

  • A warning above the results says why: the search reached its read limit, ran out of time, or could not read part of the range.
  • A line under the timeline says its bars or their colours may undercount.
  • The filtered facet counts show a plus sign (+), meaning the count is a floor.

Seeing everything

Narrow the time range, or add a filter on severity, message type or source.

Results by offset stop at the first 10,000. To reach older events, narrow the time range or add a filter.

docs.title: Column Configuration
docs.text: Click the Settings icon in the toolbar to open the column configurator. Toggle columns on or off and drag to reorder them. Your column preferences are saved in your browser.

docs.title: Viewing Artifact Details
docs.text:
Click anywhere in a row to open the Signal Details window. The detail view shows:

  1. Summary -- Key fields including timestamp, source, destination, severity, and stream
  2. Raw Data -- The original log entry or event payload in JSON format
  3. Graph View -- A mini graph showing the artifact's relationships with nodes (IPs, domains, hosts)
  4. Enrichment -- GeoIP data, threat intelligence matches, and other enriched context

docs.title: Grouping the Timeline
docs.text: Use the timeline's Group-by menu to split the bars by a field. Grouping by Client IP or Server IP groups by the actual addresses, IPv4 or IPv6. A number with no stored value, such as a missing port, is its own "unknown" group. The Group-by menu no longer offers Alarm Rule. The page remembers your choice in your browser.

docs.title: Geographic Visualization
docs.text:
When artifacts contain IP addresses with GeoIP data, a world map heatmap appears above the results table. Countries are shaded by artifact volume, and country flags appear next to geographic data in the results.

Internal IPs

Private IP addresses (RFC 1918 ranges such as 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, and 192.168.x.x) do not have geographic data and will not appear on the map.

docs.title: Saved Searches
docs.text:
Save frequently used search criteria for quick access later.

  1. Configure your search term, filters, and time range
  2. Click the Save icon in the toolbar
  3. Enter a descriptive name for the saved search
  4. Click Save

To load a saved search, click the Folder icon and select from your list of saved searches.

Auto-delete after (days) sets when a saved search ends: the day it was created plus the days you choose. 0 means it never expires. From 1.2.0 this setting is honoured. Before 1.2.0 a saved search could lose its contents 7 days after it was last saved, whatever this setting said, and a search lost before the upgrade cannot be recovered.

docs.title: Sharing Searches
docs.text: Saved searches can generate a share link. Recipients who have access to the same organization can open the link to load the exact same search criteria in their browser.

docs.title: Exporting Results
docs.text: Click the Download button in the toolbar to export the current results. Exported data includes all visible columns and respects your active filters and time range.

docs.title: Creating Work Units from Search
docs.text:
When you identify artifacts that require a coordinated response:

  1. Click the Add to Work Unit icon in the toolbar
  2. Enter a Work Unit Name and an optional description
  3. Optionally choose a work collection to add the work unit to
  4. Click Add to Work Unit

The new work unit holds up to 50 artifacts from the current search results.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
• Use specific field filters rather than broad keyword searches
  • Narrow the time range to the smallest window that covers your investigation
  • The search page prefetches the next page of results in the background for faster navigation
  • Results are cached briefly to speed up pagination through the same result set

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• On WFA appliances and the Compose bundle, a search that takes longer than about 17 seconds fails with an error. A long time range with few or no matches can take that long. Narrow the time range or add a filter.
  • In the Signal Details window, Escape does not close the window while its field search has focus. Use the close button.
  • A search with a filter applied row by row reads a bounded number of the newest events in the range. If that is spent before the page is full, the search stops and says so, so a rare match in a long time range can be missing.

docs.title: Vrax Threat Intelligence
docs.text: Import the threat-intelligence reports your Vrax account holds, and see them beside the nodes they mention.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Vrax (app.vrax.io) publishes completed threat-intelligence reports to its customers. An administrator gives the appliance a Vrax login. The appliance then:

  1. Pulls the reports that login is entitled to, for your industry and region, on a schedule.
  2. Stores them on the appliance.
  3. Shows the stored reports that mention a node's addresses, domains, URLs or file hashes in the node's detail window.

It is a one-way import. The appliance sends Vrax your login, your industry and region, and an optional date. It never sends a node, an address or an indicator from your data. Nothing it stores changes a node's classification, a score, a work unit or a report.

There are two separate connections. You can use either or both:

Card Credential What it reads Vrax threat intelligence Your Vrax username and password Vrax's completed reports Vrax feed (MISP) A feed credential: an Auth ID and a secret Vrax's feed in MISP format

docs.title: Where to Find It
docs.text: Navigate to Search > Node Enrichment. The page is headed Node Enrichment Settings, and both Vrax cards are on it.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Action Required Permission Set up, test, run and delete a connection signals:manage See the Vrax panel in a node's detail window signals:read

There is no separate permission and no licence feature for Vrax. The import is available at every tier.

docs.title: Setting Up the Report Import
docs.text:
Use a dedicated Vrax user

Vrax recommends a dedicated Vrax user for each customer, with permissions limited to this feed. The appliance stores the login, so a user that can do nothing else limits what a leaked login could do.

  1. Open Search > Node Enrichment and find the Vrax threat intelligence card.
  2. Choose the Industry and Region your Vrax account holds.
  3. Enter the Vrax username and Vrax password.
  4. Choose the Poll interval: 1 hour, 3 hours, 6 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours (the default), 2 days, 3 days or 7 days.
  5. Turn on Import Vrax reports and click Save.
  6. Click Test connection to send one validation request. The result can take up to about 90 seconds.
  7. Click Run now to start a pull at once.

When a login is already saved, leaving both credential fields empty keeps it, and entering both replaces it. The login is stored encrypted and is never shown again.

docs.title: Setting Up the MISP Feed
docs.text:
1. On Vrax's Subscriptions page, create a feed credential for this appliance. The same page lets you rotate and deactivate credentials.
  2. Open Search > Node Enrichment and find the Vrax feed (MISP) card.
  3. Choose the Industry and Region, and enter the Vrax feed Auth ID and Vrax feed secret.
  4. Choose the Poll interval, turn on Read the Vrax feed and click Save.
  5. Click Test connection to request the feed's list of events once, or Run now to start a read.

The Auth ID may not contain a colon. Neither value may start or end with a space.

A feed with many events takes more than one run to read in full: one run reads at most 200 new or changed events. Run now continues it sooner.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Status Meaning Idle Nothing has run yet. Save, enable and click Run now. Running A pull is in progress. Last run succeeded The last pull finished. Last run partly succeeded It finished, but some records could not be read or stored, or a limit stopped it. Refused Vrax refused the request. See below. Cannot reach Vrax The connection failed, timed out or got a server error. The stored reports remain available, and it retries after a wait. Rate limited Vrax asked for fewer requests. It retries after a wait. Settings not valid The stored industry, region or login is not usable. Choose them again and save. Unexpected response Vrax answered in a form the appliance does not read. It retries after a wait. Held back (size check) A pull would have removed too much of the stored data, so nothing from it was applied. Nothing is lost.

docs.title: A refusal stops the schedule
docs.text:
Vrax answers every authentication failure with the same page, so the appliance cannot tell a wrong password from a wrong industry, region or plan. The card says "the credentials, the industry and region, or the plan may be wrong".

Repeated failed logins can lock a Vrax account, so a refusal stops the automatic schedule. No further automatic pull runs until an administrator saves new credentials or changes the industry or region. Run now still tries once when you ask.

docs.title: What Appears on Nodes
docs.text:
When a stored report or feed event mentions one of a node's values, the node's detail window shows a panel headed "Vrax reports that list values of this node". Each entry names its source, Vrax REST import or Vrax MISP feed.

  • The lookup reads the data stored on the appliance. Nothing is sent to Vrax to look a node up.
  • Only external values are looked up. An address in your own network is never looked up.
  • When no stored report mentions the node, the panel is not shown. An empty panel would read as reassurance the data cannot give.
  • The panel lists at most 20 reports and says "Showing N of M" when more matched.
  • Everything Vrax wrote is shown as plain text. A link is offered only for a plain https address.

docs.title: Deleting a Connection
docs.text: Delete connection removes the saved credential and turns the connection off. With the box ticked, it also deletes the reports or events, the indicators and the sync state stored for that connection. The other connection's data is not touched.

docs.title: Network and Security
docs.text:
• The appliance contacts only app.vrax.io on port 443. Allow outbound HTTPS to it if you use either connection.
  • The import does not use an environment proxy. An appliance that reaches the internet only through a proxy cannot use it.
  • Redirects are never followed.
  • Credentials are sealed with the appliance's encryption key, AUTH_CONFIG_ENCRYPTION_KEY. If you replace that key and lose the old one, enter the credentials again.
  • An appliance that cannot reach app.vrax.io keeps what it stored and shows the status. Nothing new is fetched until the next check.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The routes are under /api/v1/vrax. The MISP feed's routes are under /api/v1/vrax/misp.

Method Path Permission Description GET /v1/vrax/connection signals:read Settings without the login, the sync status and counts, and the last test result PUT /v1/vrax/connection signals:manage Save settings. enabled and interval_minutes are required. DELETE /v1/vrax/connection signals:manage Remove the login. ?purge=true also deletes the stored data. POST /v1/vrax/connection/test signals:manage Run one validation request in the background (answers 202) POST /v1/vrax/sync/run signals:manage Start a pull (answers 202) GET /v1/vrax/reports signals:read The newest stored reports. ?kind=misp lists feed events. POST /v1/vrax/lookup signals:read Look up values in the stored data GET /v1/vrax/misp/connection signals:read The feed connection's settings and status PUT /v1/vrax/misp/connection signals:manage Save the feed settings DELETE /v1/vrax/misp/connection signals:manage Remove the feed credential. ?purge=true also deletes the stored events. POST /v1/vrax/misp/connection/test signals:manage Test the feed credential POST /v1/vrax/misp/sync/run signals:manage Start a feed read

No response, header, log line or error carries the login or the feed secret.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Context is as current as the last successful check. An appliance that cannot reach app.vrax.io keeps what it stored.
  • The two connections are separate. Each organization has one login connection and one feed connection. They store their data separately, and a refusal on one does not stop the other.
  • No proxy support. See Network and Security.
  • A refused login is not retried on its own. See A refusal stops the schedule.
